I accept the minister's statement. However, I do not think it destroys what I have said. The minister's office knew that the members of the committee were coming to Ottawa, but the minister was not there to meet them on either of the two days they were here. The minister has given what he considers to be an adequate reply to my statement. It is a matter of the extent to which it is accepted. I am not denying the accuracy of the minister's statement. It is a question of the weight to be given to it.
Questioned by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in the house, the minister offered all kinds of excuses. He said that the committee had met at length with officials of his department. The point is that the Indian representatives did not want to meet officials. The Indian people, with some justification,

June 19, 1969
Indian Affairs
feel they have met enough officials. They wanted to meet the minister. They were elected representatives, a highly responsible and competent group. The minister owed them the courtesy of doing everything in his power to be able to meet with them.
Let us be frank about it. There is the suspicion the minister intends to introduce his white paper or statement about the Indian Act without consulting with this group or other recognized spokesmen of the Indian people. If I am wrong in that, I will be delighted to hear the minister say so when he rises to participate in this debate. If the minister is allowed to get away with that, he will then be able to argue that his hands are tied, his priorities are set by his statement in the house, and he will then be unable to deal with the real problems as the Indian people see them. If he does that it will be a tragic betrayal of the confidence the Indian people had begun to develop and bad been encouraged to develop in the motives of this government. It will indicate that the government continues to distrust the Indian people. It will be exactly the same kind of runaround the native people of Canada have been receiving for years from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
There is no reason for the minister to take this course. There is every reason for him not to take it. If he makes his statement without consulting fully with this committee and other representatives, he cannot claim to have a consensus among the Indian people. He cannot expect the Indian people to co-operate with him. He cannot shed or defeat the resentment of the Indian people against the department and the reputation of the department for continued colonial behaviour.
This government generally has a habit and a reputation of secrecy and silence. In no department is silence more serious nor frankness more required than in the Department of Indian Affairs. Yet this minister has been more guilty than most of evading direct questions in the house and of avoiding meaningful meetings and discussions with representatives of the people he is supposed to serve.
I would like nothing better, Mr. Speaker, than to be proved wrong in the statements I have made.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED CONSIDERATION OF THIRD REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one thing about which there can be no debate is that the Indians of Canada very deeply distrust all governments of Canada. In the last couple of weeks the Indians of [Mr. Baldwin.!
Ontario have been demonstrating, protesting and demanding the resignation of the minister responsible for Indian affairs for the province of Ontario. The Indians of Manitoba recently picketed the health services centre provided for them at The Pas. The Indians have been vigorously protesting the plan of the provincial government, financed jointly by the province of Manitoba and the federal government, for the development of power resources on the Nelson River. This will mean the forced movement of some 600 or more Indian people from South Indian Lake who have demonstrated they have no confidence in the provincial government of Manitoba.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The Indians of Canada have demonstrated they have no confidence in the federal government. They have no confidence in the Department of Indian Affairs that supposedly looks after their interests. They have made repeated demands for an adequate opportunity to express their points of view with regard to the Indian Act and everything else which affects them.
Despite repeated statements by the minister that he would be making a definitive statement this session on the governments' position it now seems that he will be making that statement so late in the session that members of parliament and representatives of the Indian people will not have an opportunity to discuss adequately before parliament adjourns the white paper that he will present. The other day I was told that the minister will be making his main statement on June 24. If the session finished next week there will be no time to discuss it. He has repeatedly intimated that the white paper will deal essentially with the government's views in regard to revision of the Indian Act. He shakes his head. We could demonstrate this quite easily by what he has said, and much more easily by what he has not said.
For I do not know how many years, but certainly long before the minister was appointed, the government has been promising to introduce legislation setting up an Indian Claims Commission. Where is that commission? Where is that legislation? Maybe we will hear something about that in the white paper, but certainly there will be no such legislation this year.
As I understand the Indians' position they really do not want to discuss the Indian Act or the provisions of an amending bill until the government deals with more fundamental
June 19, 1969

issues which they think are important, namely, the systematic ignoring, the systematic flouting and the systematic and unilateral revision of the treaties made with them by former governments, by the British government before Canada became a self-governing country, treaties which the Indians feel were binding not only upon themselves but on the government of Canada, whether the British government, the provincial legislatures before Confederation, or the federal government since Confederation.
As early as the royal proclamation of 1763 the basic right of Indians to hunt and fish was recognized by the government responsible for the administration of this country. In the Jay Treaty the right of Indians to cross the border from the United States into Canada and from Canada into the United States, and to bring with them their household effects without being obligated to pay customs duties on them, was recognized.
But what has happened? Through a series of court decisions made by white men's courts, where Indians were not represented by counsel who understood the law, their traditional rights guaranteed under treaty have been constantly whittled away. Under the Migratory Birds Convention Act, agreed to by Canada and the United States, the right of Indians to hunt out of season has been restricted. I suggest this is completely wrong. It is immoral that the rights of a group of people, guaranteed by treaties, should be reduced by the unilateral action of a government which supposedly represents those people.
I am not an expert in this field but I have heard conservationists argue that it is necessary to control hunting by all people, including Indians. Indians have told me that they do not kill anything close to the number of animals shot by white hunters for sport and recreation. If it was necessary to restrict the rights of Indians in this field it ought to have been discussed with them, and compensation should have been provided for them. We have nothing like that.
Now we have the recent actions of the Department of National Revenue. In recent years Indians crossing the border at Cornwall have been required to pay customs duties on household furnishings brought with them, a practice that was not followed for virtually all of the first 100 years of Canada's existence. Again that was done without consultation with the Indians of Canada. It is no wonder they are unhappy. It is no wonder
Indian Affairs
they do not trust Canadian governments any more.
A recent British Columbia Supreme Court decision holds that the Fisheries Act has restricted the right of Indians to fish. This is a right they have always had. It is not difficult to argue that Indians no longer depend primarily on hunting and fishing to earn a living. But there is an important principle involved. It is that rights given to the Indian people of this country in treaties negotiated by the government of Canada, or by the government of Great Britain before we became an independent country, should not be abrogated, restricted or reduced without consultation with and agreement of the Indians involved.
It is not my duty today, nor do I have the time, to record the systematic way in which the Indians of Canada, the original inhabitants, were pushed from pillar to post until eventually they were pushed on to reservations in the least productive and useful areas of the country, to which they have been re-tricted ever since.
In view of what has been done to them, in view of the conditions which have developed, the shabby way in which they have been treated and are being treated, in view of the fact that the earning power of Indians is probably not more than a quarter of the national average, in view of the abysmal health standards of Indians, in view of the fact that less than 100 Indians in 1969 have had enough education that they may attend Canadian universities, the Indian people are saying that what they want is for the federal government to set up an Indian Claims Commission which will look at what has happened to them, assess what we have done to the Indians, and assess the damages which Indians have had to bear as a result of the treatment they have received from the white people of Canada.
e (3:50 p.m.)
Governments have been promising the Indians for years that an Indian Claims Commission would be established. Where is that commission? When have we heard even a formal or official statement on the part of the minister that such a claims commission, on which I would hope there would be a majority of Indian members or at least a substantial percentage, would be established? Indian representatives on such a commission would understand the problems of the Indians and could articulate the desires of these people so

June 19, 1969
Indian Affairs
that we could begin for the first time to compensate the Indians for the tremendous injustices which have been inflicted upon them in this country by past Canadian governments and the people of Canada for more than 100 years.
The Indians of Canada feel very strongly about what they consider to be the complete ignoring of the rights they were guaranteed through treaties negotiated freely on the part of the white people but not so freely or knowledgeably on the part of the Indians. Because of this feeling they believe they must have a claims commission which will consider the problems of the Indians and assess the kind of compensation to which they are entitled. In this way these native Canadians could begin to function as first-class citizens.
In spite of the claims of the minister and the Department of Indian Affairs that these Indian people have never before been so widely and thoroughly consulted, the leaders and representatives of the Indians have made it clear that they are completely dissatisfied with the consultations and the steps that have been taken. Let me put on record a resolution which was passed at the national conference of the Indian Act held in Ottawa in the last few days of April, 1969. That national conference brought together about 100 of the top leaders of Indian communities from British Columbia to the east coast. This is what this resolution says:
The new Indian Act will be our magna carta.
This appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail of April 30, 1969. The article went on to state:
Its impact will be more closely felt by Indians than by government. It can be our passport to equality and opportunity. Or, it could be just another compromise solution to a long-term problem.
Later the article refers to the resolution and states:
The new Indian Act must reflect the real interest of the treaties. It must stipulate the government's commitment to its obligations. The Indian people, through their legitimate organizations, should be given the opportunity to consult meaningfully with Indians across Canada, to develop their own Indian Act for (the government's) consideration and not vice versa.
That resolution is very clear. It is written in the kind of language which even this minister ought to understand. The representatives of the Indian people who met at that national conference are not satisfied with the consultations which have been held. I do not want to be unfair, and I do not think the 
representatives of the Indian people are hostile to the minister personally, but they certainly are not satisfied to leave the drafting of the new Indian Act to the top officials of the Indian Affairs Department. In their opinion, and I agree, they have consistently betrayed and ignored the interests of the Indian people.
These people believe it is the view of the top bureaucracy of the Department of Indian Affairs that the Indian people are not now ready to participate in the real decisions which have to be made if their conditions are to be improved. These people believe that the top bureaucrats of the department feel that the Indians are not ready today and will never be ready to participate in these decisions. Certainly they do not believe they will be ready in my time or in the time of the present minister who is a few years younger than I.
These native Canadians are completely and unanimously resolved that they will no longer leave their fate and welfare to this bureaucracy which has so consistently and so often betrayed their interests and their desires. They are calling on the government to change its whole approach to the problems of the Indian. To spell out this change they have asked first of all for a reassessment of consultation with the Indian people and what the rights given to the Indians under the treaties really mean in the 1970's rather than what they meant in the 1600's when the treaties were signed.
They insist that the government bring in legislation to establish an Indian Claims Commission with Indian representation and give the Indians an opportunity to appear before it with adequately trained technical staff including lawyers, sociologists, anthropologists and historians. They could then present to this commission the rightful claims of the Indians in respect of which they demand compensation for more than 100 years of wrongs. They feel these claims result from mistreatment by the white people of Canada.
Lastly, the Indians of Canada insist that the minister, not on his own or with the department, rewrite the Indian Act in a way which will not suit the Department of Indian Affairs only but, more importantly, the Indians themselves. They insist that the Indian Act be revised not simply through consultation, which simply means the officials will listen to the Indians and then go back to their offices and draft the legislation. They want to be given the opportunity to rewrite the act
June 19, 1969

themselves with staff capable of doing the job they require. They know what their problems are and they know better than white people what must be done if their condition is to be improved.
The Indians would agree that they do not have all the answers, and I am sure they would be the first to admit they will probably make mistakes. The minister surely must agree that they could not possibly do worse on their own than we white people have done for them for the last 100 years. Let me urge the minister and the government to make an effort to meet the demands and reasonable requests of the Indian people of Canada.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED CONSIDERATION OF THIRD REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject now under discussion is very important as we are dealing with the largest area of the Canadian territory, even though it is sparsely populated.
However, this part of the country is inhabited by people who were the first Canadians and who are perhaps increasing the most rapidly in number in spite of a relatively high mortality rate and a much lower rate of longevity than that of other Canadians as a whole.
I would like to quote a few statistics on this subject.
Thus, in 1965, for Canadians as a whole, the average age at death was 62, while it was about 20 for Eskimos and about 36 for Indians. Furthermore, infantile mortality in 1966, for Indians and Eskimos in the Northwest Territories, was 108.8 deaths per 1,000 living births for the Eskimos and 46.2 for the Indians, as compared with 23.1 per 1000 for the whole of Canada.
This means, Mr. Speaker, that in spite of a rather limited development, from both health and sanitation standpoints, in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and in Northern Quebec and considering also the rather high mortality rate of these people, who had sharply declined in number at the beginning of the colony, their condition has greatly improved since the first half of this century and it is now developing at a very rapid pace.
Therefore, we must pay a great deal of attention to these territories and to the people who are widely scattered in this part of the country which is not easily accessible to the officials responsible for education, health, housing, employment and so on.
The Progressive Conservative party is asking today, in the course of this debate on
Indian Affairs
supply, to consider especially the third report of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. This report deals with matters relating to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
Employment, education, housing, sovereignty in the Arctic, community centres, crafts, hydro-electric power in the North, in Dawson City-which may be considered as a tourist spot-those are so many matters dealt with by the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development during the present session.
I am a member of that committee, and on two occasions I had the opportunity to visit several centres in the Northwest and the Yukon Territories and my attention was drawn to certain points specifically referred to in the report.
For instance, in the field of employment, I was particularly struck by the lack of interest shown by employers, who take part in the development of the natural resources in those territories, towards Indians and Eskimos, in order to arouse their interest, to hire them, to promote their self-fulfilment and give them jobs in mining exploration work, for instance, or even in strip mining operations.
There is also in the Northern Territories some logging operations in which Indian and Eskimo manpower could be interested. I think the government should take some specific steps to have those corporations hire as many people living in that area as possible. Even if they have to be displaced at times to be closer to their jobs, I think this would be worthwhile. In respect of welfare assistance to Indians, a report recently published by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development shows that 39.1 per cent of treaty Indians are living on welfare assistance. In other words, 9,883 employable heads of families need help.
I therefore feel, Mr. Speaker, that this is an important matter, which requires consideration and the seeking out of solutions. To my way of thinking, the solution lies in inciting companies to hire Indians and Eskimos.
As for education, to which our committee has also given consideration, we have been told that educational methods are constantly improving, more specifically in the field of basic education, but that there is also a growing tendency to provide these people with vocational training.
The government seems to show more willingness to supply such vocational training, which can best benefit Indians and Eskimos

As for employment, pressures should be brought to bear in order to urge mining and other companies to hire local manpower as much as possible so as to improve their standard of living.
We must also concern ourselves with the housing problem in those areas. I think that the government had made substantial progress in that respect. Homes have been and are being built for Indian and Esquimo families, in order to provide them with more comfort in those cold lands. But I wonder if we have adequately taught the Indians to maintain their homes. I believe that we have failed to show them how to maintain their houses. I have noticed over there that houses which are as strongly built as our own houses in the South were considerably worn out within a few years' time, to the extent that they practically became unfit for living. In the past, we have shown too great a lack of interest in those territories to claim everything that is there, not only on the islands, but also in the surrounding waters. We will have much to do in the next few months and years, in order to take hold of those territories and to develop them as much as possible to become their true owners. speechtext:
As I listened to the debate opened by hon. members opposite, Mr. Speaker, I frequently thought I could hear myself speaking. I thought this particularly when emphasis was laid so clearly on attacking the past performances of all governments during the past several decades. I recognized the attack on the developing bureaucracy. I recognized the emphasis on a past which is indeed infested with grievances, as well as the emphasis placed by many speakers on the crucial importance of Indian affairs.
In this respect I was reminded of the private member's bill I introduced into this

interested. The Indian choice is to be a contemporary person in Canada today while remaining an Indian. Indeed, it can be said of Indians today, I think, that they recognize that continuity as Indians and the preservation of an identity can be achieved only by entering into the mainstream of life as a contemporary person.
This, as I have said before, is a momentous turn in the lives of all of us in Canada. It is a significant and historic decision that is being made in Indian communities and means that they themselves must be centrally engaged in all of the decisions that implement that particular goal.
One product of consultation will, I believe, be that full and equal citizenship implies a planned and phased reduction, if I may use that term, of the special legal and administrative arrangements that today perpetuate separateness and which in themselves become discriminatory. It means consulting Indians on every phase of the process of eliminating over a time the Indian Act and the special department whose functions, I believe, can better be performed by other federal government departments. It also means consulting Indians and the provinces to ensure that the Indians become citizens of the provinces and receive a full range of services as well as accept the obligations of other provincial residents. It means a general decentralization of administration so that Indian communities will control, for example, as much of their own lands, economic development, education and other functions as do other Canadians through their own local government and the agencies of the provinces.
Self-determination brings with it new obligations as well as the benefits of freedom. Only through consultation and understanding will the Indian people be able to share in decisions as to the extent and pace of change that they wish to bring about. Full and equal citizenship means that Indian associations must also be brought into the discussions, because they can perform an essential role in terms of projecting the consensus of Indian communities. As I have mentioned before, hon. members will note the great progress the Indians have made in consultations with the provinces, particularly in the west, and how the issue has now been joined in the province of Ontario.
This will mean that the government will have to supply funds to the Indian organizations to enable them to do their job. They will need the assistance of expert personnel and
Indian Affairs
resource trained people so they can study and fully understand the implications of going down one path or another to meet their goal of full and equal citizenship. It will not be an easy path to follow, and all of us will be confronted with many dilemmas.
Success will depend not on our enunciating a new policy but on the people themselves adopting such policy as their own. They cannot do this unless their own organizations are in the position of fully discussing with their own communities the meaning of change. We cannot hope to get a full response to new policy orientations unless we cope successfully with the complex issues and attitudes surrounding the question of treaties, claims and grievances.
The Indian treaties, apart from engaging the honour of the country, have for the Indians an enormous symbolic value, even though today the mainstream of federal policy and programs flows not from the requirements of the treaties but from the Indian Act and other sources. The deep importance that the Indians attach to the treaties naturally leads to a suspicion that major policy or program changes or shifts in the federal government mix of services may threaten the position of the treaties. Therefore it is essential that the new policy announcements and changes, which we now await, provide in themselves for intensive and close study by Indian communities and organizations of the treaty provisions and past grievances, and also of their relevance to the needs of the future. This has not been done hitherto. Both the past and the future should be viewed in a single context or as a single package. Settlement of past grievances, which is absolutely necessary to progress, should be part of the plans and programs of the future.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I believe, as a result of attending consultation meetings across Canada, that the Indians are ready to re-examine the past, not as a barren exercise but in order to balance the experiences and grievances of the past with the needs and possibilities of a fulfilled future. Continuing consultation is the only way in which the views and objectives of the Indian peoples as a whole can be made known and it is the only way in which the government can bring about a realignment of objectives. If we are to give our native peoples full equality as citizens and if special status and discriminatory aspects with regard to Indians are to be phased out, these people
10422

June 19. 1969
Indian Affairs
must be assured that they are embarked on a course which will bring success. They can only have that assurance if they themselves are involved in every phase and stage of that process as it develops.
I have tried to emphasize the need for consultation and flexibility, as have all hon. members, in dealing with this question. Without going into details may I again stress that there is an absolute necessity for us to introduce social and economic programs of major magnitude to underwrite new government policies. It is not enough for us to remove from our law discriminatory provisions, to unwind, so to speak, the Indian Act, and to transfer certain functions from federal to provincial power. Even if all this is done after there has been consultation it will not be enough to remove the legal and administrative restraints blocking the way to equality. Equality in this area will not emerge if we do not recognize that some people are starting from farther back than others in their march toward equality.
We shall have to develop special programs of an economic and social nature and those programs will have to have for our Indians a substantive meaning. Our actions must proclaim, too, that we mean what we say about the continuation of the Indian identity. We will have to orient some of our programs of assistance to make sure that what is valuable in Indian culture and in contemporary forms of Indian expression survives. We have not done this in the past. Indians will need assistance to keep alive their contemporary spirit and the contemporary form of their traditions. They want to keep alive their expressive and performing arts. I place that very high on the order of priorities. Only if we give our Indians that assurance and only if we assure them that the course we are embarked on will meet with success in the social and economic sphere will equality emerge. Only in that way can the Indian identity continue to exist.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the
opportunity this afternoon to speak for a few minutes about the welfare of the Indian people of Canada. This year, 1969, when Canadians have often heard the phrases, "the just society" and "the age of participatory democracy", our country has been facing a problem that requires immediate attention, namely, the problem of the emergent Indian and Eskimo. The non-Indian world must be alerted to what it has not done in the past and to what must be done in future.

As a member of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development it has been my privilege to travel from place to place in our great country and become better acquainted with the problems of our native peoples. Many meetings have been held during the past few months at the standing committee level. Also there have been many meetings in which the minister, his officials and representatives of Indian groups participated. What have been the results, Mr. Speaker?
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) spoke this afternoon and expressed grave concern about the government's tardiness. They complained that no positive conclusions have been arrived at with respect to proposed government policy on amendments to the Indian Act and with respect to the Indian Claims Commission which our first Canadians have long been waiting for. I must emphasize it is high time that the government moved more quickly and brought about action that will place our Indian and Eskimo peoples-my remarks, have mainly to do with our Indians although I am also concerned about Eskimos-on an equal footing with the white people. Personally, I am pleased to see that the Indians are taking initiatives to help their cause. They have organized the National Indian Brotherhood and the Indians recently held a conference in Ottawa in April which some 100 Indian leaders attended. In other words, the voice of the Indian wilderness has begun to ring from coast to coast. The Indians are beginning to give notice to Canadian society as a whole that they are emerging at last as a significant political force.
In my hand I have a pamphlet written by Mr. Boyce Richardson, a writer for the Montreal Star, who has put in phraseology more skilful than that at my command certain aspects of the Indian problem. I wish to read part of page 7 of the pamphlet. The heading at the top of the page is, "Race Has Shown Marked Success In Surviving Incredible Battering". The article following says in part:
The Indians of Canada, like those of the Americas, have made a remarkably tenacious effort of survival. They survived, first of all, a systematic effort by the white man to destroy them, an effort which culminated in the series of treaties under which the Indians ceded almost the whole of Canada in return for a promise to set aside certain Crown lands "for the use and benefit of Indians."
Since then, for 100 years, the Indians have survived the white man's assumption that they
June 19, 1969

were a vanishing race who would disappear in the fullness of time.
They are not a vanishing race, but a rapidly multiplying one. The present population of 250,000 is increasing at 5 per cent a year, a rate that would double the population in 14 years. This rate of increase is likely to become even faster, for today 60 per cent of the Indian population is under 21, and already considerable pressure of population is developing on the 6 million acres of Indian reserve lands.
I visited a number of reservations in my constituency and saw that the Indians who have accepted the white man's medicine- family allowances and social welfare benefits^-are multiplying at such a rate that soon there will be no room on the reservations for all the Indians who wish to live there. I presume the same can be said for many other areas of this country. Indian leaders themselves say that we should absorb at an accelerating rate our native Indians into the mainstream of Canadian society and make sure they have the same status as the white man. In the long run that is the only way out of our difficulties.
It is true that many Indians are suspicious of the white man because of the many promises the white man has broken. All the same our leading Indians realize that there are great advantages in allowing their children to be educated. In some academic fields our Indians could take the lead. Other Indians hope to take advantage of our vocational training facilities and learn trades which will help them to find jobs in society. Once they have jobs they will soon have sufficient status.
In future I hope it will not be necessary for us to have an Indian Act. Several Indian leaders have said to me, "You know, you discriminate against us by having an Indian Act. Why do you not have a French act or a Ukrainian act, or other acts covering other ethnic groups in the country?" I can understand the logic behind such remarks. We are segregating the Indians by having an Indian Act. They do not wish to be segregated from the rest of society. They do not want a special status. The Indian is a proud man, Mr. Speaker. He merely wants a chance. Let us see that he gets it. In the meantime the government is responsible for rectifying some of the ills our Indian people are suffering from.

I now wish to quote from the article by Mr. Richardson which is headed, "Finds treaties, act provide no guarantee as expected".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this debate, as in the previous day's debate, there have been some thoughtful and constructive things said from all sides of this house in relation to our Indian people. Pee okoke sun nika mamook wawa kope huloima iktus, nika mamook wawa kope hiyu siaaah kah cole chahko illahee.
In connection with the north, I will deal specifically with one section of the committee's report, namely that dealing with Arctic sovereignty. The committee heard evidence indicating that Canadian sovereignty over the islands of the Arctic archipelago to the continental shelf in the Canadian Arctic is well established. However, the extent of sovereignty over waters within the archipelago is less certainly defined. The committee's recommendation is that prompt and positive action by the government is required to define the extent of Canadian sovereignty.
In these few minutes that I have I wish to suggest what that prompt and positive action should be. Essentially, we should primarily draw base lines headland to headland to include the entire archipelago and declare all the waters within those base lines to be Canadian waters. We cannot stop at this point because it would not be common sense to exclude the shipping of the world from passing between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans if this proves feasible. There should be an accompanying statement to our issuance of the maps showing the base line co-ordinates. In this statement Canada should proclaim that she recognizes the rights of ships of all nations to safe and innocent passage, not innocent passage alone, but safe and innocent passage for reasons I hope to make clear later in my remarks.
In my opinion, Canadians and Canadian governments have never had enough interest in their northern territories. They never had enough appreciation of them. For most of the years that the Territories have been part of this nation we have just occasionally reminded ourselves that there is something up there in the attic that is nice to have but we know very little about it. As Vilhjalmur Stefansson

once said, if you can find any Canadian university graduate to offer you ten ideas on the north, at least nine of them would be wrong.
To be fair, there has been an immense improvement in the attitude of Canadian governments in the past 15 years. There was some awakening of interest during the years of the St. Laurent government, a considerable increase during the years of the Diefenbaker government and an interest through increased participation continued during the Pearson government. It is continuing to accelerate with this government. This is revealed in the annual budget figures in many ways. I will not deal with it, but I think it is felt here and it is also felt when you go into the north. We are taking more interest.
In some matters we are simply not taking enough interest. That is my feeling in the matter of our claim to the waters of the Arctic archipelago. We are not moving sufficiently fast or in a sufficiently positive way.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I would like to take a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, to deal with the history of territorial claims, but not with the history of our land claims because they are not in dispute. Canada essentially followed the system adopted originally by the Czarist government of Russia and since followed by some other nations, the sector theory. We took the limits of the nation's borders east and west and we extended lines in a more or less pie-shaped form up to the North Pole. The Russians took the view and still take it-they are an extraordinarily zenophobic nation, and I am not suggesting we should follow them in this-that everything within the sector lines is Russian territory. I, myself think, and from my reading believe, that most experts in international law find it difficult to conceive of a nation claiming ownership of packs of ice and even open water hundreds of miles from the nearest land.
The Canadian view was slightly different. The architect of it was Senator Poirier, and he pressed for it about the turn of the century. The Senate eventually caused the government of Canada to make a declaration. The Canadian position was that we laid claim to all the lands which might be discovered within the sector enclosed by the lines. At that time we did not think very much of territorial waters. It was not an issue, but it is becoming an important one.
Although we have belatedly taken action, and after five years of delay the government
June 19, 1969

is at least moving to draw the baselines and enclose the inland waters of the Pacific and Atlantic coasts, we are still neglecting the Arctic-yet we do consider them our waters. I quote here from a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the house on May 15, found at page 8720 of Hansard, where he was quoting with approval the statement of a former Canadian minister of northern affairs:
The area to the north of Canada, including the islands and the waters between the islands and areas beyond, are looked upon as our own, and there is no doubt in the minds of this government, nor do I think was there in the minds of former governments of Canada, that this is national terrain.
If it is national terrain, and I am speaking now of the inland waters, how precisely are we going to define it, unless we draw baselines and issue maps to the other nations which say clearly, "These are the limits of Canada's inland waters, and outward from these limits we claim three miles as territorial waters plus an additional nine as an exclusive fishing zone?" Of course this may be disputed, but Canada's claim to the archipelago and its waters does not rest upon one point alone. It does not rest merely upon effective occupation, although we have had that and it is undisputed.
There is also ground for the Canadian claim in that the islands are a natural geographical extension of the continental land mass which is Canda's. Without going into the detail of the theory there are precedents for waters within archipelagos to be claimed as a nation's internal waters. There is now a precedent for drawing baselines headland to headland, from island to island, and even from rock to rock, as has been done in Norway. Norway has established beyond dispute baselines of 40 miles. Well, if 40 why not a base line of 80 miles, or 120, or 150 or more? In the Arctic there are one or two places in which the baseline might have to reach an extent of 100 miles to pass from point to point, but we do have considerable legal support for drawing such extended baselines.
I have mentioned before that we have more of a claim than mere effective occupation of the Arctic. There are other claims which strengthen us, and there is one I have not yet mentioned. We have a specific historic claim to those waters because in 1906, when Canada was having one of its rare spasms of interest in the north, we sent the Canadian ship Arctic under Captain Bernier into those waters specifically to establish our claim to them. He came upon a foreign whaling fleet in there-
Indian Affairs
Norwegian and American. He obliged them in those waters to observe Canadian regulations as to the taking of whales, and to pay licence fees. Further, he collected customs duties from those whalers on what was at that time probably considered open seas by the nations of most of the earth. Nothing could have been done more clearly and effectively to establish Canada's claim to those waters.
The equivocation came about in 1969, and not in 1903, because until we draw those baselines and display them, what does our claim to these waters really mean? This summer the American ship Manhattan is going to attempt to force her way through the Northwest Passage from east to west. When she enters Lancaster Sound at what point will her captain say, "I am in Canadian waters"? Will he say it at all? Will it be three miles seaward from a baseline drawn between Cape Liverpool on Bylot Island and Cape Cockburn on Philpots Island? It won't be if we don't say so. And if not there, where then? At what point in the passage of Lancaster Sound will the Manhattan be in Canadian waters, or at what point in Viscount Melville Sound or McClure Strait if she gets through to McClure? I say this because the pack ice from the Beaufort Sea will probably block that way, in which case the Manhattan will likely go down the Prince of Wales Strait. There will be no dispute at that point because at its narrowest it is only six miles across and we can claim three miles from each side.
But without baselines around the outer perimeter of the archipelago our claim to these waters is formless, and other nations can legitimately ask us, "where exactly do you make your claim?" Probably some nations might even undertake to tell us where they think our claim should be, and I do not think they will be generous if they make the choice. All this concern about the waters of the north and our sovereignty there has been sharpened because Prudhoe Bay, the great oil discovery, is transforming much of Alaska. With good fortune we are going to make a similar discovery in the Panarctic operation.
The Manhattan project finally has focussed our attention clearly and precisely on this question which we must answer. I would like to review that project briefly, although most hon. members by this time have probably read of it. The Manhattan is a supertanker of 115 thousand tons. She is being reinforced and fitted with a modified form of the Canadian Alex Bow ice-breaker plough. She

is owned by Humble Oil Company. The intention is to see if she can move through the Northwest Passage to Prudhoe Bay. If she can then it is expected that Prudhoe Bay oil can take the short way into the eastern United States or into Europe, because the shape of our planet is such that the Arctic actually is quite close to Europe. It surprises some people to learn, for instance, that when leaving Vancouver and driving as close as you can drive to Coppermine you go 1,000 miles inland and about 2,000 miles north, yet Coppermine is as close to Yokohama as is the city of Vancouver.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Perhaps there is no point in speculating on the chances of the Manhattan making this passage, but I have heard them estimated at about 50-50. She has a tremendous forward thrust, about 45,000 horsepower. Her reverse power is considerably less, something below
10,000	horsepower. If she does become wedged in the ice it will be necessary for the John A. Macdonald and the United States icebreaker West Wind to break her free. The experiment would then probably be a failure. Let us hope it is not, because if regular shipping could move through the northern ice this would be a great thing for all of us; not just the United States but Canada as well.
There is one interesting point in this regard, and that is whether the United States government asked our permission to put this paramilitary vessel, the coast guard cutter, through the Northwest Passage. When the minister appeared before the northern development committee some time ago he was asked this question, and he said: Yes, in effect they had. Under the Canadian-United States defence agreement it is common practice, or acceptable practice, for the United States government to inform us in the event of planes or ships entering Canadian air space or waters, and that this in effect constitutes permission. I hope the minister is correct and that the United States has adopted that interpretation, but I am by no means convinced that it has adopted that interpretation.
Those who saw a recent story in the New York Times in which the president of Humble Oil was discussing this great project-it was lengthy and interesting-would not have found anything to indicate that Canada was involved in any way. It is hard to believe that Canada is even aware these ships are passing alongside Canadian islands. His statement as to these waters is that there is an opportunity for a great international waterway to be

opened up by his ship. Personally, I feel it is a great pity that Canada is not putting the Manhattan through instead of the United States. Of course, it would be expensive, but so is our experiment with Panarctic. We have to risk some money to make money up there. I think it would have been worth it.
In 1913 when Steffanson was fully financed by the United States geographic society to explore the Canadian arctic and Sir Robert Borden was informed, he would not tolerate it. He put Canadian money into the expedition and it became a Canadian expedition with United States participation. In any event, the Steffanson explorations were Canadian.
I think Canadians are hoping that this crossing of the Northwest Passage will be successful. We should hope that a great waterway does open up there so that our ships and the ships of other nations can use it. You may ask why, then, should I be concerned as to sovereignty over these waters if we are to welcome the ships of other nations and offer innocent passage. There are no great fish resources there. There are some but they do not appear to be extensive in the Arctic. Why should we concern ourselves? Let's just draw the three mile plus the twelve mile straight lines along the shores of individual islands, and if the lines do not meet leave them as international waters. One might ask that, but there is more than one reason we should be concerned. I am going to outline one or two.
If we establish sovereignty, it will increase our responsibilities in the Arctic. If regular traffic develops through the Northwest Passage this country would be responsible for installing navigational aids and these, like everything else done in the Arctic, could be very expensive. I am pleased to learn that our Department of Transport is making a study of the cost of installing a Decca system in the Northwest Passage. Again, I feel the government is moving a little more slowly than it might. Our position would be better if that Decca system were put in on those islands by ourselves. We could put up a semipermanent system along the side of the passage. We could then have charged the Manhattan a nominal fee for moving through on our Decca system. This country will be responsible for installing such a navigational system.
This is the more dangerous aspect of the situation. We may find ourselves tempted to say to the United States: These are your ships
June 19, 1969



and this is your oil you are moving out. You put the system in, you make the expenditure and then this will be your system. Now, we come into the dangerous part which involves territorial rights to the land. Let me quote briefly from two authorities who appeared before the northern development committee, one Dr. Carr and Dean Maxwell Cohen. Am I running short of time, Mr. Speaker?

I will be very brief, Mr. Chairman. I should like to quote what Dr. Carr said on this point. He recently wrote an article on the economic aspects of the Yukon. When I asked him what future threat to our sovereignty might exist, he said he saw no threat to sovereignty over the land mass of Canada for the moment. He then said:
I think we just simply have to keep moving in the direction of insuring our sovereignty. I did not mention that the factors that tend to assist the encroachment on our sovereignty are improvements in transportation, air transport, under sea transport and various new developments in technology.
He went on to say:
In those vast spaces, it would not be difficult for other countries to set up studies or research units here and there and eventually obtain squatter's rights and move on. The point I do make is that we must be more energetic and do more in terms of services for the north now than we used to when it was so difficult to reach the north.
Dean Cohen of McGill University said very much the same thing to the committee. He put it in these words:
It is possible to argue that as technology improves exploitation must equally improve on the part of Canada to reinforce the idea that we effectively occupy the area and if we did nothing in the Arctic except visit when in fact technology provides now for real chances for exploitation, we might be weakening title if the sector and other theories did not support us.
We must consider the possibility that the United States might wish to put a navigational aid system in the Northwest Passage and that we might be sorely tempted to let them do that, to our own detriment.
In closing I wish to refer to another point. The Manhattan is comparatively small as a supertanker. She carries 112,000 tons. The latest ship to be built for Gulf Oil by the
Indian Affairs
Japanese has a 300,000 ton capacity. The Manhattan is larger than the Queen Mary and if stood on end would be taller than the Empire State building. The latest ship built for Gulf is far larger than that again. I would ask hon. members to think of the Torrey Cannon disaster in the English Channel when this small tanker spewed out her oil and poisoned the beaches in England and France. She was a small tanker.
I would ask hon. members also to consider that the chief danger in a passage through the north is being trapped in the ice and crushed. What would happen if a supertanker the size of the one recently built for Gulf Oil were caught in the Arctic ice, crushed, and lost
300,000	tons of oil? It would mean that 75 million gallons of crude oil would be spilled out in the waters with temperatures from 33 degrees, to 34 degrees. I ask you to consider the size of the problem that would face us, the terrible expense and the almost incredible damage that would be done to the ecology of the Arctic. This is the reason we should have control of these waters and the power to determine what ships come into them. We should be able to determine that these ships are safely built and that disasters of this sort do not happen. We cannot have control unless we have sovereignty.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate. I shall be rather brief. I should like to begin my remarks by dealing briefly with the department of Indian affairs. I think it can be generally concluded that there exists today a great deal of mistrust between officials of the department of Indian affairs and the Indian people. The Indian people have witnessed a huge bureaucracy build-up within the department. As I pointed out a few days ago in my speech on the budget, in personnel alone an increase in excess of 50 per cent has taken place in the department in the last three years.
Much of the dissension which exists today between the Indian people, the government and those concerned with the administration of Indian affairs is due to poor liaison, lack of understanding and lack of a true, sincere and sympathetic approach in earnestly working, through co-operation, to overcome the numerous difficulties which exist among our Indian people. The concept of paternalism which has been the philosophy of the department of Indian affairs has to be scrapped. In its place I believe we must adopt a philosophy of sincerity and sound national conscience in order to overcome the social and economic inequalities which exists between the Indian and the white communities. The situation that exists today can only be termed as harmful in many ways when one looks at the complete picture of our Canadian society.
I believe the role of the department of Indian affairs must include the reparation of some of the government's shortcomings in the treatment of Indians. It must also include the neutralization of the ethnic tension which exists between the white and the Indian peoples. In addition to the normal rights and privileges of Canadian citizenship, I believe it is reasonable to assume that the Indian community possesses certain additional rights because they are, after all, charter members [The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
of the Canadian community. I believe the Indian affairs branch has a special responsibility to see that these additional rights in so far as citizenship is concerned are respected, and that the government and the Canadian people are educated to accept these standards. Rather than dictating to the Indian people what the department of Indian affairs thinks is right or wrong, the officials of the department should be concentrating upon the development of education, upgrading living standards and providing employment opportunities. This would demonstrate a true feeling of trust and understanding. At the present time the Indian affairs branch is a massive stumbling block which prevents the Indian people from achieving their hopes and aspirations. The Indian community is discriminated against through a rigid interpretation of policy. We should be placing the emphasis on development through a humanistic approach.
We cannot legislate rigorously. There are no cut-and-dried policies created through legislation which can provide a humanistic approach to achieving the aspirations and ideals of our Indian peoples. I submit-I am glad the minister is in the house this afternoon-that one step which would improve the relationship and understanding which exists between our Indians and the Indian affairs branch would be to immediately commence the recruitment of Indian personnel to man many of the offices in the department. As far as I am concerned, no one has a better understanding of the problems of Indians on or off the reserve than the Indian himself. I believe that no one in our society is more aware of the poverty, social injustice and economic degradation of our Indian people than the Indian himself. Therefore, I urge the minister to consider this matter in order that Indians may have better opportunities, greater responsibility and a more realistic stake in their destiny.
I should like to deal briefly with treaties and their interpretation, particularly in so far as they concern health and welfare services. Although the treaties between Her Majesty Queen Victoria and the Indians of British North America were instituted and negotiated by men of good will in what they collectively considered to be the best interests of the Indian people, there is no doubt in my mind that the treaties are now woefully outdated, impractical and in many cases meaningless. For example, many sections of these treaties are obsolete, such as one plow for every ten families; a yoke of oxen for every band, and a suit of clothes for the chief every third
June 19, 1969

year. Clauses respecting hunting and fishing rights, health and welfare services and education are grossly outdated and have lagged far behind the national progress of this country.
It is generally concluded, through the interpretation of these treaties, that health services were to be provided by the federal government as long as the sun shines and the rivers flow. But what have we today? With the advent of medicare we have much confusion, apprehension and dissension. We have an atmosphere of mistrust and an environment in which the Indian Association has urged all treaty Indians to boycott enrolment in the Alberta medicare program. I should like, Mr. Speaker, to quote from the Edmonton Journal of January 13 in order that the evidence in this regard may be on the record. The article is entitled "Indians urged to boycott medicare in premiums row" and reads in part as follows:
The Indian association of Alberta is urging treaty Indians to boycott Albert's medicare plan until the question of premium payments is resolved.
The association maintains that medicare premiums must be paid by the federal government as part of their treaty rights respecting guarantees of health care.
Harold Cardinal, spokesman for the association, said the federal health and welfare department has indicated it will pay premiums for treaty Indians only on the basis of need.
The Indians Affairs Department, meanwhile, claims national health and welfare must pay any premiums necessary to ensure coverage on Indian reserves.
"It's not an issue with us," Mr. Cardinal said. Indians feel the federal government must pay the premiums for them, and they don't care which department does it, he added.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
He said, however, Indians wish to ensure that their treaty rights will be protected. They also want assurance that their medicare premiums are not turned over to the provincial government, if the federal government carries out its policy of turning medicare back to the provinces after five years.
"We want assurance that the federal government will pay all our health costs in future, as they have in the past," Mr. Cardinal said. This is part of the historic treaty rights, he added.
Farther on, the article reads:
There has been "confusion" at the regional level between the two departments, over the question of premiums, Mr. Cardinal said. He said he hopes the two ministers will clarify the matter.
In the meantime, treaty Indians are being advised to refuse to register for medicare, he added.
Today I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) a question
Indian Affairs
regarding this specific subject and he advised me that he will be attending the Indian Association conference in northern Alberta tomorrow or on the weekend. I presume that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) will attend also. The Minister of National Health and Welfare suggested that he will urge the Indians to enroll. I should like to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the Indian people in my province want some clarification of this matter, and rightly so. Certainly, they want some assurance from the federal government and some guarantee that payment will be made for the health services as prescribed under the respective treaties. After all, health is of prime concern to the Indian people. They were assured that their health services would never be curtailed. Now, they are being asked to produce an indigent or hospitalization card.
I think that some clarification is due to them to indicate how we are going to classify those who are indigent and those who are not.
My contention is that those who are living on the reserve are entitled to be granted health services under the terms of the treaty. In my own province of Alberta the government has built a so-called medicine chest. However, on many occasions it has been reported to me that many of these people are denied these services and facilities. One individual from the Saddle Lake reserve suggested that they are asked to be sick on certain days. "If I am sick on the reserve on Thursday, I may have to wait until next Wednesday to get into the hospital", he said. I believe that this is a breach of promise and I hope that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Minister of National Health and Welfare will clarify this matter. I hope that it will be clarified well before the end of June because, as hon. members may or may not be aware, the medicare program is due to go into effect in Alberta on July 1. The deadline for enrollment is the end of June.
I should now like to touch briefly on some aspects of the economic development and of the conditions on reserves as well as the plans and programs the government intends to implement to overcome the deplorable conditions which exist there. I think that the Indians, and the public in general, cannot understand why the government has continued to disburse funds on welfare and mere subsistence allowances. I believe this money would be much better spent on developing work projects and developing industry on or

June 19, 1969
Indian Affairs
near the reserves which would make possible the employment of Indians and thus make them self-sustaining. This is certainly one of the areas in which I believe the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion could play a very useful role. I think that officials of the department should take a long hard look at the possibility of encouraging and promoting industry on or near the reserves. After all, this is one of the major problems with respect to the employment of Indians on reserves. Indians, just like any other human beings, want to spend their evenings and weekends with their families on the reserve. Therefore, I believe there is a great deal of merit in developing industry in or near the reserves.
The housing, the sanitation and the water supply in the majority of reserves is deplorable. There is great poverty. For example, in my own riding of Vegreville, in which the Saddle Lake reserve is to be found, the same conditions exist. I have had much correspondence with the minister with regard to housing. He was good enough to despatch two of his officials to the reserve and we made a survey. Our survey revealed the fact that we need 100 houses on the reserve to meet the demand in the next five years. That comes to an average of 20 homes a year. The average number of homes that have been built in the last five years has been seven or eight per year. We are certainly never going to catch up unless we upgrade our program. When we look at the deplorable situation, the low standard of living and the poor housing on the reserves I believe we are fair in saying that the government and the Indian affairs branch have failed. Why have they failed? Because they have not given the Indians the opportunity to achieve their own destiny through active involvement, through participation, and through the acceptance of responsibility in discharging many of the numerous administrative, social and economic activities which exist on the reserve.
We hear it said in some quarters that the Indians have no pride. Well, they do not have too much to be proud of, particularly in view of the paternalistic approach of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I say we should give them opportunities and responsibilities and they will soon experience a deep sense of pride.
I should like to refer again to my own constituency of Vegreville and the Saddle Lake reserve. Recently, the band council embarked on a very ambitious project of

clearing something in the order of 15,000 acres of prime arable land. This project has provided employment, administrative experience and responsibility and has instilled a sense of pride in the Indians. It has had a terrific impact on Indians as is shown by the decrease in welfare. In addition, a prefab housing plant was established and is continuing to operate. It constructs homes for use on the reserve, and it also has had very good effects. It has developed an incentive in Indians to increase their skills, to take post secondary courses and, for example, to attend the school of agriculture in the neighbouring town of Vermilion. Some have also taken up carpentry. All this has instilled a sense of pride and responsibility.
These programs have been administered through the local band council and they have instilled a sense of responsibility. People are proud to have a say in their future and in their destiny. I hope that the minister will continue to encourage these types of programs because they will bring nothing but good to the Indian people and to Canadians in general.
I should like to conclude my remarks by reminding the minister that since he is in the process of writing a policy or a position paper on the new Indian Act, I hope he recognizes that Indians also are a changing people and that future policies must be flexible and adaptable to change. I urge that he incorporate and utilize the talents of our Indians to solve the numerous problems which we have created together and which have accumulated over the years. The Indians of this country are not interested in hearing any more words or seeing more complicated legislation and red tape. They want a reaffirmation of their rights and some positive action to overcome the complexities of their disparities so that they too may have the opportunity to participate in the benefits which other Canadians have had.

speechtext:
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that in suggesting that one of the days be used to examine the report of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development the opposition has shown, I suppose I might say for once, a great deal of good judgment. I am happy, as I know every member of the house is, that the opposition should have chosen this subject for discussion
June 19, 1969

today. I think the spirit which has been shown by all members indicates the concern and the honest confusion which exists in the minds of so many of us in this house, and of so many Canadians, with regard to the future of the Indian people.
We hear constant references to the Indian and Eskimo people and the circumstances which have existed in the past. We continually hear advice as to what should be done in the future. As a Canadian who is not of Indian background I feel somewhat reluctant to become involved in this debate. I believe the Indian people of Canada are beginning to show that they, too, have ideas about what their destiny should be.
What has been happening in the past two years or so, community development programs, education programs, housing programs, schemes for economic development and, what is more, the consultation which is going on between the government and the Indian people, are an indication that the Indian people are ready to take upon themselves much of the responsibility which in the past was exercised by government. The minister has promised that shortly there will be a statement on the government's position with respect to questions affecting the Indian people. I do not wish to get involved in giving advice to the minister. I will merely say that I trust the statement to be made will not become a political football. I hope it will be left to the Indian people to determine whether or not it is satisfactory. I hope it will be left to the Indian people to produce alternatives if what the government has said is not what they want. I, for one, believe the role of parliament should be limited to satisfying ourselves that whatever the Indian people want is carried out.
In the Northwest Territories, as in other parts of Canada, we have seen significant changes in the Indian way of life, in Indian attitudes, and in the attitudes of the Eskimo people. I should like to tell members of this house about a society which was formed by the Indian people in the community of Fort Smith. Historically, the Indian and Metis people of Fort Smith had a difficult time breaking into the government establishment. There was a problem of communication, a problem of economics and education. About three years ago a group of local people decided that they would form an organization to help themselves. This group, known as the Theb-ache society, assumed, in effect, responsibility for the economic development of their own 29180-6605
Indian Affairs
community. The manager of the society was a former heavy equipment operator for the Department of Northern Affairs. His work force consisted of people from all parts of the community. Race really did not make much difference. The group was able to fulfil contracts offered by the municipal government, the territorial government and the federal government. In the first three years hundreds of thousands of dollars of income were made available to residents of Fort Smith as a result of the initiative and action taken by the Thebache society.
Groups such as this could become cornerstones for the kind of creative activity, the kind of leadership which we hope will come from within a community, and I hope the government will take cognizance of this situation. I am sure any hon. member who has had experience of work of this sort can report the same kind of achievements. Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) referred to me as parliamentary secretary-I think he was intimating I was parliamentary secretary to the Minister for Indian Affairs and Northern Development. However, Mr. Speaker, as you intimated when you recognized me, I am the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I want to make this clear in anticipation of what I shall have to say in the next seven or eight minutes. On two occasions in the last few years, the committee has visited the north, once in the summer and once in the winter. I think this has been a good learning experience for members from the south who would not normally have an opportunity to see this wonderful part of Canada.
I know that in the last parliament some of the strongest supporters of the idea of northern development were members of the committee from all parts of the house. Members had an opportunity of meeting the commissioners of the Northwest Territories and of the Yukon Territory. They had meetings with members of both councils, including the appointed members of the Northwest Territories council. They became familiar, as far as the Northwest Territories were concerned, with the Carrothers report.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
By way of background, in 1965 the then minister of northern affairs, recognizing the restlessness of the people in the Northwest Territories in regard to the administration of their own affairs, appointed as Commissioner,

June 19, 1969
Indian Affairs
Dean Carrothers, to examine the future of the political, social and economic development of the north. This commission reported to the minister in October 1966.
Basically, the recommendations of the Carrothers commission were that the then administration, which was centrally located in Ottawa under federal auspices, be transferred to the territorial government and moved to the north; that the powers of the council be expanded; that the terms of reference of the elected members of the council be widened; and that government be brought close to the people. Much has happened since that period. The capital, Yellowknife, has been developed. The territorial government, the newest government in Canada, is on the ground and has taken over much responsibility of a provincial nature. But that is where it ends.
When the announcement was made of the location of the capital in February 1967, the indication was that the Federal government's position on further political development would be made known shortly. Two and a half years later we are still waiting for an announcement. The Northwest Territories council is in session in Yellowknife, and the members of that council are critical of the lack of a statement. They have said to the minister that they must hear from him; that the minister must come to the north and tell them what their political future is to be.
I believe the minister would like to be in the position to do this. He may have decided what should take place in the north; whether or not we should be divided; whether or not the size of the council should be increased; whether or not we should continue to have appointed members; whether or not the councillors should have the right to set their own indemnities. But I am more than a little concerned that up to this time we have heard nothing.
I tell the minister in all sincerity that this statement must come and has to come before the conclusion of the present council session. I say that to the minister because I believe that his relationship with the elected members of the Northwest Territories council, the appointed members and the average citizen in the north, depends on whether or not this statement is forthcoming.
I regret that I have to say this to the minister in this manner, but I believe the role of the federal government in the north during

the next number of years is greatly dependent on the kind of mutual trust and understanding that is developed between the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, his commissioner in the Northwest Territories, the Northwest Territories council and the people. In my travels in the last three or four months I have become aware that the people of the north are restless. They are looking to the minister for a statement, a statement that will show the kind of leadership that can be given in the transfer of responsibility.
I have said on more than one occasion that at this stage of our development in the north we are not talking of provincial status or quasi-provincial status. We are saying that we want the right to run our own affairs and to make the kind of decisions that affect a person's everyday life. I hope the minister is able to convince his colleagues in the cabinet that he is under severe pressure, or, if I may use the expression, that he is under the gun to produce. And produce he must. He must produce by Friday of next week.
