speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I heard many comments worth listening to on this subject affecting Indians and northern affairs. I found especially interesting the speech of the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) who touched on a subject matter somewhat different from that dealt with by other hon. members. In one sense he was promoting new ideas and I hope the minister paid close attention to him. We can do something worth while in the area to which the hon. member referred.
I wish to deal with a theme with which most hon. members dealt with this afternoon, the theme of the native peoples of Canada. I am concerned about the future of these people. I wish I had had the chance of hearing the minister's speech before making my own comments since what he has to say could easily alter what I have to say. The other day I asked him what the government's policy is in this area. I understand he will give us his answer before the end of next week. I want to make some remarks in order to make sure he does not forget that we expect him to make a statement.
A short time ago when consultation meetings were going on in Ottawa I had the good fortune to treat one Peter Dubois to lunch. He is an Indian from my province of Saskatchewan. He told me that when the Indians controlled North America they had a good educational system which was flexible and served their needs. They also had a code of morals and ethics, and an economic system. The only area in which they failed was immigration policy. He said they had a poor immigration policy. It was second class. Indians can at least joke about themselves when they look back on their history, their problems, and the mistakes they made. But they are concerned about the future.
We took their land and left them to live on reservations. We left them the poorest of poor land which they could not make a living on even if they were exceptionally able farmers. In exchange we offered them our way of life, our habits, our language, our sense of justice, etc., whether they wanted to accept these things or not. We pay civil servants high salaries to administer Indian affairs. We give aid to Indians. We call it social aid but it is charity and handouts, call it what you will.
Indian Affairs
You know, some Indians look on the department of Indian affairs as a make work project for white men. White men are making work for high priced civil servants who are not too happy sometimes about the names Indians call them.
There are five Indian reservations in my constituency. Having visited them I have become acquainted with many people. I have hired some Indians to work on my farm and discovered that Indians, too, are people. I want to discuss some of the complaints and observations the Indians have made as individuals. I would also like to deal with how the department of Indian affairs affects them by what they do or do not do. An Indian on a reserve who is idle receives a form of social aid which will help him to survive. If he tries to get ahead by farming or owning a small business, it is like pulling hen's teeth to get assistance from the department. Have any hon. members ever applied for social aid through the department of Indian affairs? It is a very awkward and slow procedure. If you want assistance in order to farm or have your own business, you might receive it this time next year, if you are lucky. Some feel it is so awkward they do not even bother applying for it.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Another complaint Indians have made to me is that Indian agents who understand them are quickly moved from the post they hold. I think this is a valid complaint they are making. These people who understand the problems of the Indians are asked to move by the department of Indian affairs. I received a complaint from a magistrate. He said the Indian cannot get drunk on the reserve and cannot afford to hire a hotel room, so where is he to get drunk but on the street. When this happens the reaction is: there's a drunken Indian; get a policeman and throw him in jail. What is the magistrate to fine this man if conditions for him are not the same as they are for the white man? If we are going to give the Indian justice, he should be treated as an equal of the white man.
The leader of the Creditiste Party has suggested a French speaking person in Quebec or Ottawa should be entitled to have his trial conducted in French. I ask the members of the Creditiste Party, if an Indian gets drunk or commits a misdemeanor in Quebec in what language is his trial conducted? It is conducted in French. In my part of the country his trial is conducted in English, not in Cree,

June 19, 1969
Indian Affairs
Huron or Montengnais. These were the original people on our continent.
I think the minister of Indian Affairs should have a heart to heart talk with his colleagues the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) as some of the work of the Department of Justice in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon is still being farmed out. There is no Crown prosecutor in that area and that is the reason the work is being farmed out. One is never sure who the Crown prosecutor will be. It reminds me of something said by the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) who earned his living as a humorist writing a column for a Vancouver newspaper. He discontinued writing the column because he found it very awkward to be in this house and still write a humorous column for a Vancouver newspaper. I am a farmer from Saskatchewan and I find it awkward to run my farm from Ottawa. I believe it is equally difficult to administer justice in the Yukon Territory from Ottawa.
I wonder if the eloquent, patrician, well paid, well educated civil servants in Ottawa really understand what the problems are out there? They should go and live with the people to understand the background of these people and the conditions they have to tolerate? In that way they may have a better idea of what justice is all about. I strongly urge the minister to look into this matter.
There is one other area which is quite disturbing to me, that is the problem of unemployment in the north. This was mentioned by some hon. members this afternoon. Although it is a problem all over Canada, it is the responsibility of the federal government to a larger degree in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. I suggest the Indians affairs branch should have personnel officers to help Indians or Eskimos when they move to a new job and change their way of living. We frequently hear of Indians or Eskimos who get a job, stay for a short time and then leave because of emotional problems or some other factor. I suggest these personnel officers could counsel these people, as it is very awkward when they cut themselves off from one way of life and then find they are unable to do well in another.
Another matter I would like to mention is something I have been told by young people. These are people who are attending university or are graduates. They are clever people and they have done well. However, I am surprised at the bitterness among them and their lack of trust in not only the Indian affairs branch but of all white people. As a member

of parliament, I was also included in that sense of distrust as they really do not trust anyone. They feel that many years of promises have not brought them what they wish. It may be that the general public have not accepted or recognized these young people. Possibly they still treat them as second class citizens; I don't know. This is an area in which we should improve our relations with these young people.
I would now like to deal for a moment with the matter of Arctic sovereignty. One of the reasons Arctic sovereignty has come to the fore lately relates to the possibility of oil in that area, both on the land and under the sea, and the value of that oil. I am hopeful oil will be found in that area, as there is sediment there of the type found in Alberta and Saskatchewan. In all likelihood there will be more oil found in that area than in these two provinces combined. What concerns me in this respect is the problem of future markets.
As a wheat farmer, I have encountered a great deal of disturbance in our area because of the lack of markets. At the present time in Alberta oil is being produced at only 45 per cent of capacity. We are now developing more oil wells in the Yukon, Northwest Territories and in the high Arctic. I am quite disturbed about our national oil policy. I strongly urge the minister to announce a policy which will give some direction to our oil people because they are very concerned about this matter. The name of the game in oil is markets. If you cannot sell oil, which is expensive to produce, what good is it? We should look at it as a national resource and see that the market is developed in an orderly fashion.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)

It is a pleasure for me to voice my personal opinion in this very interesting debate on policies governing the Indian affairs of Canada.
While listening to some of the speeches made by our friends in the opposition, I have heard some very interesting statements and I have tried to listen to them with as much attention as possible.
Among other things, it has been said that the Indians should be treated the same as the white population, that their rights should be recognized and especially that ancient treaties should be honoured.
Some hon. members of the opposition have attributed to the minister some hostility
June 19, 1969

towards the Indians. It was even said that the Indians would be opposed to any legislation that would be enacted by the government until they are assured that those ancient treaties would be honoured as they should.
The minister has also been accused of not doing his duty. It has even been said that the Indians in Canada no longer have any confidence not only in the government of Canada but also in the provincial governments, and that they were deliberately being relegated to the most isolated, barren areas in Canada.
The last speaker, who is a good friend of mine, the hon. member for Battleford-Kind-ersley, (Mr. Thomson) quoted a phrase, with which I understood he agreed, saying that the Indians had a good education system and highly advanced ethics when, centuries ago, they were masters in this land.
I have great respect for the Indians. I have known several of them for whom I had much esteem, having worked with them, made trips in the North with them when I was practising my profession.
But, although I respect them highly, I also respect the ancestors of the white people. And, when I heard the remarks of the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley, it struck me as very similar to saying that when our paleolithic ancestors were hunting, gathering food to survive, they had an education system superior to ours and that we should, we, Europeans and North-Americans, go back to the paleolithic education system.
I think that in Canada, our respect and our love for the Indians are increasing. Is there an employment problem among the Indians? Of course, but this problem is becoming more and more world wide because of the development of our society, because of automation and of technological progress.
As for Canadian sovereignty over the Arctic regions, it is a very important aspect of Canadian politics which should not be forgotten. Therefore, it is good for hon. members to remind occasionally, as often as possible, the minister and the government that it is more and more necessary, at least to claim possession periodically of these far northern areas which certainly belong to us and which will later yield resources that will help our economic development.
This third report of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development is indeed most interesting and I think that every hon. member, regardless of his political party, should first congratulate the
Indian Affairs
members of this committee for the remarkable study and observation work they did during their last trip in northern Canada. It is indeed a good thing to see that, at the beginning of their report, the members of the committee mention that in the course of their northern trip they noticed a vigorous and healthy economic growth in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon.
We stress the problem of employment, as I said a while ago, because it is always an urgent problem.
There are many problems to solve, not only in the employment field but in all other fields dealt with in this report. Are we going to say that this government has not taken these last years very positive action, apart from helping the native people of Canada to solve their employment problems? The same could be said of education, housing, arctic sovereignty, friendship centers for the Indians who come to live in our cities, handicraft problems among the Indians, electric power in the north, which is in my opinion a pretty difficult problem to solve, on account of the enormous distances and sparse population in those vast territories.
There remains the tourist aspect of certain areas to be dealt with. As concerns Dawson City, when I was a member of the committee on northern affairs a few years ago, I saw that the area of Dawson City-that already old city that was so active at the time of the gold rush-is one of the most interesting as far as the tourist industry is concerned and there is still much to do there.
But having looked into the present government program and the estimates for the current fiscal year, can we say that the government and the minister do not want to do anything for the Indians? On the contrary, I think that in that field, the government is striving harder than ever.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
If we consider, for example, item L-40 in the estimates for this fiscal year, it is aimed at increasing to $4,300,000 the amount authorized for loans to Indians and Eskimos for the construction and the purchase of houses, up from $2,300,000, while in 1967-68, it was only $1 million.
For the entire program to which are allocated items 1 and 5, the estimates for this year amount to $175,159,000, while last year they totalled $135,446,000, an increase of $20,574,000. And if we examine that program and

June 19, 1969
Indian Affairs
those estimates, we will see that it is the same for all the other items.
Allow me to refer to a publication of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development which gives facts and figures about Indian affairs, and which was published a few years ago. It is obvious the figures are not recent, but we can see that already, at that time, the policy of the present government in the field of Indian affairs was constantly improving, as was the situation of the Indians and the economic organization of the territories where they live.
Whether the figures relate to Indian handicraft, education, housing (construction and repairs), we always note the same progress.
When comparing the general expenditures for 1965 and 1966, in the fields of education, welfare, economic development and administration, including the special fund of British Columbia, they amounted to about $81 million for the fiscal year 1965-66 and $104 million for the following year, an increase of over $24 million.
With regard to engineering and to capital expenditures, including the construction of roads and bridges as well as other works relating to water distribution systems in 196162, for instance, the total votes allotted in this connection amounted to $1,420,000. In 1966-67 they were $3,845,000, nearly four times more.
Regarding education, the total expenditures in 1961-62 were $6,944,000, and in 1966-67, $11,418,000, that is nearly twice as much.
As for economic development, the amount spent in 1961-62 was $446,000 and in 1966-67, $2,085,000.
As far as the housing program is concerned, government expenditures for 1961-62 amounted to $2,254,000, and for 1966-67 to $8,226,000.
I think we might say, in the light of those figures, that things could be better for the Indians and their economic development, but we are doing a great deal at the present time as we did in the past. And now the Canadian government is doing its utmost to increase even more the well-being not only of the Indian people, but of every Canadian citizen.
May I be permitted, before concluding my remarks, to inform the house of some needs that are felt by a few Indian bands in my own region, along the Lower St. Lawrence river and in Gaspe.
In Gaspe, there still exist two reserves of Micmac Indians who lived in the area already

under the French regime and account for approximately 15 per cent of the population.
In passing, I wish to say that on the Maria reserve, for instance, a new school for the neighbouring Indians has just been built and that 80 per cent of the costs, if not the full costs, have been paid by the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I would like to remind the minister that in Gaspe, on those two reserves, many houses are in poor shape. In fact, many houses have neither running water nor bathrooms or, as we say, no sanitation nor water supply.
One important question is the order of the day of the Micmac reserve of Saint-Louis-de-France, at Maria, in Gaspe. There now exists a trading problem with regard to handicraft. For a long time, if not for always, the Indians on that reserve have specialized in the weaving of baskets. Occasionally, as is the custom, they trade those for mocassins, slippers and other handicraft products with the Indians of the Lorette reserve. As far as the reserve in Maria is concerned, it could have quite an interesting market with the United States, New York particularly, at the present time. Because they have to pay high customs duties, the Indians are loath to develop such a business which would be very profitable to them. On the other hand, the chief of the reserve, Mr. Leonard Jerome, came to Ottawa recently to meet with officials of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. He pointed out that matter to his member of parliament, the hon. member for Bona-venture (Mr. Bechard). He also mentioned that products imported from Japan were advertised as being made by Indians of his reserve and that it was quite detrimental to their business.
On the other hand, Indians of both reserves and citizens as well who visit those reserves complain about the sorry condition of the highways. They would be most interested in seeing the government give special attention to their repairs and improvement.
For many reasons, I think, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development might be interested in establishing on the reserve at Restigouche a museum which would have the advantage not only of stirring up the interest of Indians and visitors, but also of developing the economy of that area.
A few years ago, the Capuchin Fathers of the parish of Restigouche, who minister to the Indians of the area, discovered the ship of
June 19, 19B9

the Marquis de Malause, a French naval officer, whose ship is reported to have sunk in the Restigouche river, in the vicinity of the reserve, during the last wars between the French and the British.
They located the wrecked ship, and they are now proceeding with further excavations.
Mr. Speaker, we feel that if the department could take some interest in this particular warship and other details related to its foundering, it might improve the status of the Restigouche Indian band, boost their economy, attract tourists and have other advantages, not only for the reserve, but for all the people of the area.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my appreciation of the minister's drive, and congratulate him on the initiative and decision he has shown whenever problems, greater or lesser, occur in the field within his responsibility. To illustrate this, I would like to recall briefly one field where he recently put up a brave and successful fight.
His efforts, among other things, without mentioning the touristic and, in particular, the economic angles, will have the effect of providing employment for some people in the Gaspe Peninsula, not only to the Indians to which I referred a moment ago, but also to the white people, to other citizens of the area.
I want to point out the positive and spirited manner the minister has displayed during the debate on the setting up of the Forillon Park.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not anticipate having the opportunity of saying a few words on this subject quite so soon, but I welcome the time now that I have it. We have under discussion a motion concerning the third report of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Like other hon. members, I was interested in the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre), who dealt with one specific item of the report in which the committee recommended that prompt and positive action by the government is required to define Canadian sovereignty.
I think it can be fairly said that the hon. member's speech dealt with that recommendation of the committee in rather concrete
Indian Affairs
terms which I found very interesting. Generally speaking, I felt his proposal was one that I would be able to support. For the most part, however, the discussion this afternoon tended to centre more on matters which are not referred to in the report of the committee. The committee report pays particular attention to the situation of the native peoples of Canada. Its report contains headings which deal with jobs, education, housing, friendship centres and handicrafts.
No one in this house would deny that these matters are important and are very real questions with which the committee should properly wrestle. However, Mr. Speaker, I feel I should enter this discussion at the point at which it was introduced this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). That hon. member introduced into our discussion an area that is not touched upon at all by the report of the committee. In my judgment this represents a serious omission on the part of the committee, which otherwise presented a well-rounded report for a committee of this kind. I am not saying this by way of criticism of the committee, because I realize there are limitations upon the matters a committee may include in its report. I mention this matter because, despite the importance of parliament being concerned with such matters as jobs, education and housing for the Indian and Eskimo peoples, the more fundamental question of the relationship of the rest of us to these people is at the core of what we should be discussing today.
All the well-meaning efforts that may have been made in the fields of housing, employment opportunities, retraining, and so on, will have missed the point unless we in this parliament are prepared to come to grips with what in my opinion is the fundamental and basic manner in which we should deal with this group in the Canadian society. Reference has been made to the fact that a statement of new policy is shortly to be forthcoming from the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien). The hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) touched upon this subject in a speech which I thought was able and constructive. He referred to the fact that this comprehensive statement of new policy will shortly be made after an intensive, nine months review.
I confess that I do not await the statement with quite the same degree of optimism as that displayed by the hon. member for York-Scarborough, because on a number of occasions when it has been said we were on the

June 19, 1969
Indian Affairs
verge of a comprehensive statement of new policy we have heard from various ministers, statements which have not lived up to expectations. The minister who now occupies this rather important and arduous post will, I hope, succeed in his portfolio and have time to get his teeth into the questions that need to be dealt with. It is unfortunate, whatever may be the reasons behind it, that for quite a long time we have not had a minister in this portfolio who remained long enough to come to grips with the problems that must be solved.
I remind the minister that since the Liberal government assumed office we have had in this portfolio, if my list is complete, Mr. Fa-vreau, Mr. Tremblay, Mr. Nicholson and Mr. Laing in rather quick succession. In the period before that we had Mr. Fulton, Mrs. Fair-clough, and for a brief period Mr. Bell. I mention this as one of the reasons for the long procrastination in really coming to grips with the essential problem of the recognition of the rights of these people, as referred to by my colleague the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Thomson).
The hon. member for York-Scarborough referred to these people having full and equal citizenship in the mainstream of Canadian life without loss of their identity. If I heard him correctly, he referred to the fact that it was not enough simply to unwind the department of Indian affairs or the Indian Act. I agree with that sentiment. I have said before in this house that in my opinion the core of this problem lies in unwinding the effects of colonialism, which covers a much broader area than that covered by the Indian Act or the department of Indian affairs.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I was intrigued by the remarks of the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley to the effect that Indians had a good economic and educational system but a very poor immigration policy. He said this with that quiet sort of humour that the Indian people display with regard to their position and relationship with the rest of us. The hon. member's remarks reminded me of a discussion I had with the people of an Indian community in my constituency. We got into a rather similar area of discussion which came to the point of my suggesting that because we call these people Indians we tend to lump them all together as it were, whereas at the time Europeans began to arrive on this continent there was no more relationship or kinship between people from the St. Lawrence Valley and those from

British Columbia, than there is today between the people of Finland, for example, and Malaysia.
I suggested to the people with whom I was talking that if Columbus had thought he had discovered China instead of India, they would all be Chinese. This remark seemed to catch their fancy and we had one of those beautiful, quiet sessions of laughing about it. I suggest to the minister that if this had happened he would now be the minister of Chinese affairs, even though this would not involve him in some of the matters in which we understand his colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) is involved.
One of the aspects of this whole situation with which the house has been called upon to deal from time to time centres on the reference to the idea of an Indian claims act. The whole question is in many respects one which should take precedence over any revision of the Indian Act or decision to abolish the Indian Act. My own experience after hearing various ministers introduce bills throughout the years on the subject of Indian claims makes me more sceptical than the hon. member for York-Scarborough as to the nature of the shining light of policy which may be expected to come from the present minister. I recall a bill being introduced with considerable fanfare on this subject in 1963. First reading was given on December 14. In due course the bill reached a stage where consideration was to be given to its terms in consultation with the Indian people. Well, Mr. Speaker, a bill supposedly based upon the results of this consultation was introduced on June 21, 1965-and it was identical in all important respects with the one which had been introduced in 1963. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) refers to the need to deal with Indian claims, but I suggest that if we are going to seek once again to deal with these claims in terms of either of the bills introduced in 1963 or 1965 we might as well forget about the whole idea.
Something much more fundamental is needed. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) said we were dealing, now with a different ball game, and this is the thought which has been going through my mind. The sweep of events in the last few years has so outdated any action contemplated so far by this parliament that we really need to begin all over again, though I realize this is scarcely possible. I should like to remind hon. members of a plan for dealing
June 19, 1969

Indian Affairs
with Indian claims which was put forward by my hon. friend from Skeena (Mr. Howard) and myself at the time the bills to which I have referred were under consideration. We advanced the idea that the claims commission should, as it were, belong to the Indians- that it should work for the Indians by presenting their claims; that it should not leave in Indian hands the work of marshalling the necessary evidence, and so on. Such a commission would constitute a real step forward in the context of the realities of the situation today.
Some hon. members may recall that when dealing with the two former bills my hon. friend for Skeena and I attempted to present a substantive amendment on second reading, one which reversed the concept of the commission set out in the bill. Instead of the commission being an agent of the Crown it would be a court of Indian claims, one which would, as far as possible, lie beyond the control of the Canadian state; one which would as far as possible be an international tribunal.
I remember arguing that such a court should be headed by someone other than a Canadian, by some judge with an international reputation, in order that the commission might operate in the spirit of the United Nations charter and might constitute a recognition that our encroachment upon the land and sovereignty of the Indian people is something for which we were prepared to compensate. It was my contention then that the flow of events was passing parliament by. Since then, the things that many of the Indians have been doing tend to make courses we have advocated in the past less relevant to the situation.
I am prepared to say now that the concept of the commission for which the hon. member for Skeena and I argued in 1963 and 1965 is less relevant today than it was then. If we could get away from a judicial atmosphere altogether it would be more in keeping with the spirit which the Indians themselves are showing today. If the minister were prepared to come forward with a policy statement making it clear that the government intended to establish a commission which would represent the Indians as their agent when dealing with the government and with the Parliament of Canada, then I would hope that in a spirit of mutual goodwill the concept of an international court of claims might become superfluous, and that we could reach, as it were, a man to man settlement with the Indian people which would settle this issue once and for all.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I am glad that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), in opening the discussion today, took an approach which I feel is essentially in agreement with the one that 1 am advancing. I also felt that there was the same basic attitude and approach to this question in the speech made by the hon. member for York-Scarborough, and I am glad of it because I think that there is a genuine desire on the part of members in all parts of this house, in the words of one of the speakers this afternoon, not to allow this issue to become a political football. I think that there are many members in the house who sense that we are dealing with something that is at the very core of our future self-respect as a nation.

I was about to conclude, Mr. Speaker. I was going to say that I think the last time there was any real sort of breakthrough in dealing with the whole matter of our relationship in this parliament and our relationship as a Canadian people to the Indian question was in the work that was done by the parliamentary committee in 1960-61. Some of the more practical aspects of the recommendations of that committee have been dealt with, at least in part, and some of the transformation that has taken place since that time stems from the work that was done by that committee. I hope that we are on the verge of a breakthrough in this area at this time. As I told the minister frankly, although I am a bit sceptical I am also genuinely hopeful that as and when he makes his statement, to which various people have referred, it will be the kind of statement that can be applauded by members in all parts of this chamber.

attributes of the constituency I represent, Prince George-Peace River, but because of the importance of this debate I am sure my constituents will support my contention that an issue concerning people deserves priority, a view which many hon. members share.
Problems and the direction of their resolve by official and unofficial bodies is so complex and divergent that there is a danger of Indians, Eskimos and whites alike losing sight of the over-all objective. Constructive dissent is necessary and desirable, otherwise consultation meetings would not have been initiated by the government. Consultation meetings have allowed members of this house, indeed all Canadians, to hear the grievances of those persons most concerned with the administration of the Indian Act, that is the Indians themselves.
It is not possible for all meetings to be successful in the eyes of all participants or observers. We have all attended conferences or meetings of one kind or another when we felt elated that much had been accomplished. We have also experienced that let down feeling when we wondered what prompted our attendance. To expect elation from each consultation gathering would be naive of both the participant and the observer.
The meetings were not controlled. It has been suggested that the discussion booklet "Choosing a Path'' prepared by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development directed the dialogue to a predestined goal. The brochure was prepared as a guide and a tentative agenda. Surely, it is common sense to pattern a procedure.
At the Prince George meeting it is recorded that Mr. H. Pierre of the Stuart-Trembleur band asked whether the meeting must follow the booklet or whether reference could be made to anything in the act. Mr. Boys, regional director of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, said that the delegates were free to refer to the act or the booklet or to present their own ideas. Unfortunately I was unable to attend the five days of discussion, but again going by the record and from my personal observation I 
know that the subjects discussed strayed considerably from the prepared guide.
Non-Indian concern for the rights of Indians has been a long time in the making. Our society's inherent virtuous manner will not allow us to accept our responsibility without looking for an excuse or for someone to shoulder our guilt.
Criticism is levelled at the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Accusations could be tolerated if we were not required to examine the record too closely. Certainly, some errors are evident, but in dealing with the subject objectively, compassion and common sense is frequently exercised in tempering the stringent regulations of the Indian Act. Considering some of the human resources, both white and Indian, with which the department has had to work, it is surprising that there are any signs of progress at all.
White society established an act that was originally designed to protect Indians. Some bands required and desired protection, but others did not. Unfortunately, all were treated alike. The same situation appears to be the case today. In presentations at consultation meetings some bands indicated that they want to go the entire way to autonomy, while others suggested partial authority and the balance did not want change.
In consideration of the desires of Indians, I suggest that the act should be flexible so as to accommodate specific regional administration.

speechtext:
The act must be amended to provide for the natural right of self-government to return to Indian communities their pride in self-reliance.
Many Indians and whites in coming up against the legislative regulations of the act have been badly bruised by their own people and by the rules. They have contributed toward awakening our conscience and should be remembered for their individual stand. However, the courage of those who remain within the ambit of the act to work for the change and development of their people is much to be admired. Laws cannot be changed by immovable confrontation. Conflict of ideas, tenacity of conviction and proof make for reasoned revision. It may take longer to proceed in an orderly fashion, but in the end the results are more firmly entrenched.
I have some problem in approaching the matter of education properly because I am unfamiliar with the content of the proposed
June 19, 1969

white paper. I feel, however, that hon. members should be made aware of the concern of Indian parents and students. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is in the process of phasing out residential schools and entering into educational agreements with provincial governments. Concern is quite high for the type of facilities to be made available in the province of British Columbia. As you may be aware, Mr. Speaker, integrated independent schools in British Columbia receive no financial assistance from the provincial government; they are self-supporting. Indian parents are of the opinion that the basic policy of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, which is, and I quote, "to purchase the services of provincial and territorial school systems for all elementary and secondary school Indian and Eskimo students as soon as possible", means that their children must attend the public school system, or if they attend an independent school that they will be required to pay all fees themselves.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
During the hearings of the committee, we received assurance from the deputy minister that Indians would continue to receive financial support for children attending independent schools. I suggest that the question of Indian education be examined closely. I would not like to see a basic policy or an act of this house be misinterpreted by administrators.
As the house will note from the report of the Indian affairs committee, members of the committee are cognizant of the role education will play in bringing about more equitable treatment for Indians. To assist all members in their assessment of present and future policies, I would like to draw their attention to the testimony of Mr. Walter Currie, president of the Indian-Eskimo Association of Canada and assistant superintendent of supervision, department of education, Toronto. His testimony appears in the minutes of proceedings No. 28 on pages 963 to 1001. I suggest all members read it carefully.
During the last debate on Indian affairs, the minister stated that provincial governments must accept responsibility for Indians as they do for non-Indians. I adhere to that principle also. Acceptance should not mean that they move from one special status to another special confining status. There must be complete equality. Non-Indian communities have a responsibility to share in the loosening of restrictions on Indians. We cannot
Indian Affairs
place the entire problem at the feet of Indian agencies. Legislation may provide equality, but people must make that legislation live.
Legislation should be the tool for directing the many programs to aid Indian-Eskimo development. It should not be a crutch for the native or non-native communities. The Indian Act does not prevent the employment of natives at current wage or salary rates; they are locked out by prejudice and by lack of understanding. Businessmen may employ Indians and Eskimos without the approval of the minister or regulations under an act.
Will an amended act provide jobs? I doubt it, Mr. Speaker. Is it also easier for charitable persons to devote a few years of their lives to bringing medical care, education, employment opportunities and to the general raising of living standards in far off countries than it is for them to direct their energies to helping our own native peoples? I am aware of the motivation and I do not wish to detract from it, but when we evaluate the shortcomings of the Indian Act we must not let it cloud the evaluation of our own social and business conscience.
In considering the third report of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, we may justly assume that members of the committee have had their work cut out from the very beginning. I am sure we anticipate a large volume of work to arise from the forthcoming white paper, but the greatest task all hen. members have before them is to advise the non-Indian community that an amended act is not a crutch. We must all strive to ensure that Indians and Eskimos gain and maintain their rights to full citizenship as citizens, not as instruments of regulation.

Mr. Speaker, there has been a great deal of discussion this afternoon about the Indians and their problems. Nothing was said against them. I have indeed nothing against their problems and I sympathize with them. There is an Indian reserve in my constituency. I would add that, while travelling across Canada, I did notice that those people are experiencing problems. Many things have been said on this subject and I do not want to go over them.
I will deal with a new problem now under review which concerns the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, namely national parks.

June 19, 1969
Indian Affairs

The former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development spoke optimistically of a program to establish 40 to 50 new national parks by 1985. The new minister, in a burst of enthusiasm, has expanded this figure to 60 by 1985. In this we wish him well. But we must also add a-

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext:
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, in his proposal to establish 60 new parks by 1985, we wish him well. But we must also add a realistic footnote to this problem and

remind the minister that since 1885 only 20 national parks have been established, of which only two have been added in the past five years. Furthermore, the present park system creates the anomalous situation whereby 94 per cent of the national parks' area is in western Canada, where only 26 per cent of Canada's population lives. I am not saying this critically; rather I wish to point out the necessity for parks.
As we all know, an agreement was reached a few weeks ago giving Quebec its first national park. Ontario's six million people are served by only three small national parks. All of this indicates that we are desperately short of national parks. Couple with this shortage our tremendous rate of urbanization and increased leisure time, and the whole situation takes on almost crisis proportions.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)

There is no doubt that national parks are necessary and I need not overemphasize the point. The people need them more and more.
Working hours are being increasingly reduced. In brief, people want to enjoy themselves. They want to observe nature, they want to relax a bit. Bar-B-Q is now a household word.
One only needs look around in the stores to realize that picnic equipment is in great demand.

We realize that the creation of a new park is a cumbersome and difficult economic and constitutional process. Negotiations between the federal and provincial governments are difficult because usually the province must first acquire the land that is to be dedicated and then turn it over to the federal government without encumberance in perpetuity. The provincial government then obviously relinquishes all claims to the property, including any claims to mineral rights. That is the present position as we understand it unless, of course, there have been proceedings that this house has not been told about or that the minister has kept secret.
Provincial governments in the past have been very jealous of their rights and hesitant about surrendering land under these absolute conditions, their reluctance stemming from the fact that they may one day decide that the development of mineral finds with timber stands is more lucrative than any esoteric benefit to be derived from an outdoor recreational facility and the concomitant revenue
June 19, 1969

generated by increased tourist traffic. The demand for compensation on the part of provinces for their lands is often an insurmountable problem. There is here, of course, an important question of jurisdiction. Canadians who frequently take advantage of the existing parks are beginning to see the results of these federal-provincial stalemates as overcrowding begins to spoil the beauty of these areas. Lack of facilities makes the park areas unattractive.
By 1985 five times as many people as today will be trying to use these existing facilities. Will the facilities be sufficient to accommodate them? We sincerely hope that the government will not continue in its present delaying fashion to wait for an overwhelming outcry of public opinion before being spurred into action because by that time it may be too late.
I have alluded to the urgency of this problem. There is one further aspect to which I wish to direct my attention and the attention of the minister. That is the question of the over-all policy considerations with which the minister guides his negotiations. These considerations are relevant to our discussion this evening because of the recent agreement that was concluded with the government of Quebc.

I want to say, in all sincerity, that we are proud of the announcement concerning the establishment of a national park in Gaspe but we are concerned about the policy of the department or the government with regard to this new project.

We welcome the announcement of the creation of the first national park in Quebec. Nevertheless, because of the manner in which the park was established we must raise certain questions. We do so in the spirit of ensuring that our system of national parks will not be weakened by a too flexible approach to the negotiations. Canadians must be sure they know what is happening. We must ask, then, what the present policy of the government is with respect to national parks. Has the Quebec agreement signalled a change in policy? If it has, what is this new policy? If it has not, what is the government proposing to do about other provinces which are not willing to turn over the necessary land without encumbrance in perpetuity?

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am about to conclude my remarks. At this time I should like to reiterate our great concern about the government's sluggish reaction to this critical problem. The difficulties in creating a national park anywhere in Canada today will be increased many times over if the current inaction continues. The future preservation and development program of our wilderness areas is simply too vital for the future of Canada for it to be subjected to a vacillating and leisurely policy.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that the minister will be able to tell us, once and for all, whether the most recent decision represents a change in policy. I know that the minister wants to say a few words tonight. It is now 9:30 and in closing I would just say that when making decisions we should not irritate the other provinces.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to take a few moments of the time of the house in order to take part in this debate which has been, generally speaking, very enlightening. It has touched on Indian affairs and northern development. Most hon. members who spoke made a worth-while contribution. Only a few adopted a partisan attitude. After the first speaker in the debate, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), had completed his remarks the house settled down to an orderly discussion of Indian affairs and did not attempt to play political football with the Indian people. Generally speaking, if one ignores the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River, this has been a sound debate.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext:
Hear, hear.

June 19, 1969
Indian Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext:
The problems of the Indian people in Canada are most serious. Immediately after being appointed Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development one year ago I tried to find solutions to these problems. I looked at the problems and got in touch with the Indian people of Canada. Last July we launched a series of consultations and for the first time in Canada's history Indian people in Canada were able to really participate in the elaboration of a new Indian policy. The results of the consultations were by no means perfect. The format of the meetings has not been perfect. At any rate, the meetings gave the Indians a chance to express their views. We discussed all aspects of the Indian situation in Canada and, after 17 meetings across the country, we had the last meeting in Ottawa about a month ago. There the representatives of all Indians of Canada put forward their views to the public and to the government of Canada.
The time has not come, Mr. Speaker, for the government to respond. As I said in the house not long ago, that response will be ready soon. We shall have a new policy on Indian affairs and I will announce it in the house before the end of this session.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext: When?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext: I think that next week I will be in a position to make that statement.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext: Why not make it tonight?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext:
Because we must be courteous to our Indian people and because, being more courteous probably than the hon. member would be if he were in government, I wish to distribute the relevant documents to) the leaders of the Indian communities so that they have them in their hands at about the same time as hon. members here have the contents of the documents. Also there must be an opportunity to have the text of the document printed, and it will take a few days before it is ready. We decided after a year of consultation that it is time to offer to the people of Canada, including the Indians, a new policy. We have heard from the Indian people that they are proud and are willing to take their future into their own hands. They want to make more decisions.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
There has been a certain pattern existing in Canada for over 100 years. We feel we have to make many changes. Personally, I feel quite frustrated most of the time because of certain

situations. For example, when Indians wish to borrow a few thousand dollars from C.M.H.C. they are obliged to get the signature of the Superintendent of Indians of Canada, who happens to be myself, before they are able to get the money they need. This is the sort of thing that requires change. We have to permit the Indians of Canada to make more decisions at the local level. The policy of Indian affairs to be tabled next week will reflect this attitude of the government.
Today, we heard about the problem of Indian treaties. I have said many times that we intend to respect all aspects of these treaties. However, there are some problems. We must find the mechanism to permit the Indians to know what their rights are. A significant aspect of our last consultation was the establishment by the Indians of Canada of their own committee to study their treaty rights. I think this step will have a great influence on the new policy that has been established and will be made known next week.
I do not wish to take too much time of hon. members by commenting on the Indian policy because this will be made known next week. We think this policy is the best approach to permit the Indians of Canada to be economically and socially equal to all citizens of Canada and at the same time be in a position to keep their own traditions of culture which they have had in Canada since before the white people came to this country.
I will not refer to all the points raised by hon. members in the house today because many of these have already been dealt with in committee. Hon. members asked questions regarding education, housing and other matters. Most of these questions were answered by my officials or by myself when we appeared before the committee.
I want to thank all hon. members who have participated in this debate. I wish to assure them we will not overlook any of the proposals they have put forward today. We intend to make a complete and objective review of the Indian policy. This is one of the most difficult social problems that we have in Canada. These problems should not be approached on too much of a political basis, but in the spirit of proving to the first citizens of our country that we are willing to offer them a new deal in a Canadian society.
I would now like to deal with a point raised by an hon. member regarding employment. I wish to inform the house that we have offered summer employment in my
June 19, 1969

department to all university students of Indian origin. The department has hired 87 of these students. We made certain we had a position to offer to every student of Indian origin who cared to apply. I feel this is a very good response from the Indian population.
Many other matters were discussed by members of the committee. I wish to refer to the speech of my good friend, the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) regarding the territorial waters of Canada.

I think, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin has explained the situation very well.
Of course, the problem is quite serious, but I want to reassert here that there is no question at this time about the sovereignty of the government, of the people of Canada over the North, the Arctic Islands and the northern continental shelf.
The only unsolved problem is the territorial waters problem, which is most complex and cannot be solved easily and unilaterally. There are territorial waters problem in all parts of the world today, and as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has pointed out so ably in his statement of May 15, 1969, we must be careful and act in such a way as to ensure the maximum protection to Canadians, without for all that infringing upon international jurisdictions.
I wish however to thank the hon. member for his very positive contribution which will certainly help the government assess the situation. He showed that he has thoroughly looked into the subject and that he was very concerned with the problem. I must assure him that the government too is very concerned with the matter, all the more as now, because of the fantastic development in the North in the past few years, in connection with the potential development of oil and mining resources, it is extremely important that Canada resort to every available means to retain for itself and its citizens control over resources and the access to resources.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

With your approval, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) touched on the problem of national parks. The government has committed itself to an effort to establish more national parks in this country. The hon. member said that in the last five years we had established only
National Parks
two national parks. If I may be permitted I wish to point out to him that in the period from 1957 to 1962 when his party formed the government not a single new national park was set aside for the benefit of all Canadians.
Personally, I am happy to see that the people of Canada are beginning to realize it is important to set aside land for national parks for use by future generations. I accepted the hon. member's contribution to the debate and the spirit of conservation in which he made it. I point out we must be conscious of the fact that in 15, 20 or 25 years from now there will be a great lack of land available in North America for recreational purposes.
As I say, the government is willing to establish more national parks but we need the collaboration of the provincial governments to do so. We have established two national parks since the government took office, and I am glad to mention that in a few weeks from now we will have a new national park on the west coast of Vancouver Island. I would publicly like to thank the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) who, as the former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, was the main initiator of the movement that will bring to Canada probably what will be the best coastal park in North America.

speechtext: In keeping with the mood of the house and the minister's own very generous mood, could he tell us what is the position at the moment with regard to the second national park on the west coast of Newfoundland, a project that has run into some difficulty with the government of Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was coming to that point because I want to show the hon. member that we are concerned and that we are proposing to have more national parks in the future. One of them will be the second national park in the Bonne Bay area of Newfoundland. I have spoken about the new national park on the west coast. We are negotiating with other provinces about more national parks.
I was happy with the talk I had the other day with the Premier of Saskatchewan, who is now ready to permit the government to go ahead with the establishment of another national park in that province. I hope that in

June 19, 1969
National Parks
the weeks and months ahead we will find agreement on other national parks in Saskatchewan. We are working to establish another national park in Manitoba, and lately we took steps to establish the first national park in Quebec. May I say I am very surprised that the opposition questioned that move. Through ARDA we have achieved a plan to have Quebec's first national park established. We were flexible in our approach. We were not too flexible. In the past we made special arrangements with other provinces. We were obliged to make a special arrangement in B.C. because of a particular problem. I do not think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) would disagree with what I am saying.
We had a special problem in Quebec but through the ARDA agreement we have succeeded in establishing a national park there. We have stated in this house that this was a particular case and that we do not intend to proceed in the same manner in the future. I think the people of Canada are happy that for the first time we will have a national park in Quebec. You know, Mr. Speaker, it will be a great contribution to the development of the tourist industry in that part of the country. It will be one of the most fantastic parks in Canada, and will be very good for the province of Quebec.
At present we are having some discussions with the government of New Brunswick to establish another national park in that province. We are proceeding quite rapidly, but I do not know when I will be in a position to make a definite announcement. However, I found the government of New Brunswick very easy to deal with.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext: What about Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext:
We have three small national parks in Ontario and we are having some discussions with the province right now. We are not progressing as fast as I would like in Ontario, and I think the members from Ontario should raise hell if they want more national parks in that province. I need some backing in order to achieve that. I hope the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) will help me achieve that goal.

Mr. Speaker, I should simply like hon. members to realize that, at the present time, visotors to national parks are increasing at the rate of 15 per cent every year. In the United States, where there are 250 million inhabitants with more and more leisure time,

they just cannot handle all those who wish to visit the national parks. As a matter of fact, there is such a big demand that people have to wait for hours and days to visit the parks.
In view of the fact that it is still possible for us to put aside those big green spaces for future generations, it is my opinion that we should act now, for, in 25 or 50 years from now, it will be too late.

I forgot to mention that we are negotiating to establish three more national parks, two in the Northwest Territories and one in the Yukon. The people in those areas are generally receptive to the idea, and in the gallery tonight there is the mayor of Fort Smith, who is a great advocate for national parks in the Northwest Territories.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not take up too much of the time of the house. I have explained the situation about national parks. I touched on the situation in the north, but I forgot to refer to the problem raised by the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange) about the statement on development in the Northwest Territories. It is not yet ready, but I hope it will soon be ready. I will not tie my hands by trying to specify any date, but lately we have made great progress in cabinet on it and I hope soon to be in a position to make a statement. However, it may take a few more days. I can assure members of the house that we will have a new policy that will permit the people of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon to participate more in the administration of their own affairs to determine the quality of their own lives. I hope to make that statement after tabling the white paper on Indian Affairs.
In conclusion, I wish to thank hon. mem-ers for their contributions to this debate. It was a very worthwhile one and we received good advice. The spirit of the debate was not partisan. I hope members of the house will retain that mood in the future.
June 19, 1969

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the brief minute left at my disposal I would like to say that we are all looking forward with great anticipation to next week when the minister is going to be forthcoming on matters about which he has been asked for many months. I would say to him that despite how hard he has tried and how much he has listened, it will take a great deal of effort on his part and a great deal of compassion to compensate even in part for the grievous, egregious errors made for many years in the administration of the affairs of our Indian and Eskimo people.
I speak as one who has no Eskimo constituents and whose Indian constituents in terms of quantity are negligible. But I was impressed by many things in the report. I thought the reference to Arctic sovereignty was one of the most pusillanimous statements I ever cast my eye upon. I noticed also the reference to unemployment among Indian and Eskimo people. I say to them, and about them, they are suffering from a malaise that is affecting the whole of Canada today, especially the young students.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
In particular I accept the minister's invitation to raise hell about national parks. He talked about Ontario, Saskatchewan and New Brunswick. I would like to remind him that for many years discussions were undertaken by his predecessor with the government of the province of Prince Edward Island in reference to a national park there. I am sure that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing), a man of excellent judgment, splendid taste and a real feeling for this country, will understand that there is land available in Prince Edward Island, that gem of tourist attractions; that area par excellence for tourists. I may say, with a burst of utmost unselfishness, that this is so because it is not even in my constituency. I say to the minister that it would be a fine thing if he and his department would move more rapidly in their discussions with the province of Prince Edward Island to establish a park in the eastern part of the province. I see the minister nodding in agreement.
Our province, with its somewhat restricted tax base and its narrow range of industrial capacity, has as its most expansive and most expandable industry, the tourist industry. The Dominion Government could do a great deal by developing a second national park there to provide facilities comparable to those now provided for nearly a million visitors
National Parks
who come to the national park which is located partly in my constituency and partly in the constituency of my friend the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean). This is why I am so unselfish. Here we could do something that would enable the people of Canada to see the beauties of this garden province.
In my gentle way I do raise a little hell with the minister, to use his rather off-expression which no Prince Edward Islander would use. I urge him to exercise a little alacrity in discussions with the province of Prince Edward Island in respect of one of the few areas in which we can expand our economic base, namely tourism. This will offer an injection of substance, support and encouragement, and I urge this upon him with all the sincerity at my command.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: COMMONS DEBATES AFTER RECESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with some amazement tonight to the attack by the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) on the parks policy of this government. The hon. member must be living in a never, never land because here is the record. Members know of the proposed parks in western Canada, in British Columbia, the west coast of Vancouver Island and the Long Beach area-one of the scenic highlights of the whole nation. In Saskatchewan we have proposed parks in the vicinity of Val Marie and on the South Saskatchewan. In Manitoba there are parks in Flin Flon and the Bloodvein River area. There is going to be a park in northern Canada, and that project is now under discussion. There is a park proposed for the Newfoundland Bonne Bay area. I could go on and on to give proof positive. We could go into the Gaspe and New Brunswick and consider the Kouchibouguac area, and I hope I am pronouncing that correctly. In Nova Scotia and a park in the East Point area.
This all is proof that the minister has demonstrated a keen appreciation of the need for a comprehensive and diversified parks system in Canada. His predecessor also made a distinguished contribution to the parks policy of this country. Some people nurture the mistaken notion that there are millions of acres of undeveloped land in Canada, and they dismiss the need to set aside on a systematic basis additional park reserves at the national level. This theory is nonsensical. I am glad to acknowledge in the house that the minister appreciates this fact. In no sense does Canada possess unlimited recreational resources. The total area per capita in Canada appears large but over 80 per cent of the land

is poorly accessible northern tundra and nonproductive forest.
It is encouraging to note that the minister does not aspire to being a defender of the status quo in respect of park policy. Regardless of the criticism which has been directed at him-perhaps indirectly by the opposition -he is perhaps better aware than any of us that a recreation explosion lies ahead, far beyond the numerous demands for recreational facilities we have seen in recent years. The population growth, the rise in individual and social mobility, the increase in urbanization, the increase in personal income and the increase in leisure time available are going to bring increasing pressure on our resources of recreation.
For every person using Canada's recreation land in 1960, there will be four people using the same land in the year 2,000 A.D. This is not a doubling, this is a double doubling. Some 10 million people are going to visit our national parks each year, and some 50 million people will visit these parks each year by the year 2,000. This will mean a five-fold increase from now until the year 2,000.
The argument is advanced that in economic terms the value of our parks is open to question. More than ever we are going to witness a struggle between those who see in all lands, wherever they may be located, an economic resource measured purely in terms of extractive riches, and those who see in our national parks a heritage of immeasurable value which must be preserved for all generations. I find myself in agreement with the latter philosophy, and I know that the minister is in agreement as well. This encourages us.
Even in economic terms, the year 2,000 may see Canada's parks and our wilderness area as being the most valuable resource in this nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 29, 1969, I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) a question in which 1 requested assistance to prevent bankruptcy among some Quebec farmers.
Mr. Speaker, at no time in its history has the province of Quebec experienced the application of such a weak and unsteady agricultural policy as the one it is subjected to at the present time.
In that region where I live, the Eastern Townships, farmers are leaving the land at an alarming rate. In nearly all the parishes around Lake Megantic and in parts of the Compton constituency, there are parishes where at least six farmers, on a weekly average, abandon their farms. This is a disaster unheard of before. This is certainly attributable to the agricultural policy even though much was expected from this policy which did not materialize.
The government's dairy policy is resulting in disastrous consequences for the farmers. This policy is forcing a great number of producers to abandon their farms.
The minister did not tell the farmers the whole truth when subsidies were granted and his policy is now producing terrible and irreparable damages.
For instance, subsidies for a 100,000-lb. quota of milk would be worth $990, or 99 cents per cwt. The penalty for shipping an additional 50,000 pounds would be $260, that
June 19, 1969	COMMONS
is 52 cents per cwt. This penalty of $260 should be deducted from the net subsidy granted for a 100,000 lb. quota, which would reduce the subsidy to $730. Therefore, it is really a penalty, because it contributes directly to reducing the net subsidy.
All this is frustrating, especially the policy, on account of its great rigidity toward progressive producers. In other words, it strikes more directly the farmer who wants to increase his production and to improve the use of his resources.
This is detrimental to efficiency in the dairy industry.
The situation is disastrous in the province of Quebec and I believe in the whole of Canada as well, because a policy of punishment cannot succeed. In a way, punishment is meted out to the farmers who wish to increase their production. At one time, the government was asking the farmers to extend their holdings in order to make their operations more economic, today they are punished for having done this.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Not only the small farmers who produce less than 50,000 pounds of milk leave the land but also those who produce 150,000 and 200,000, although for many reasons, they would be in a better position to survive from an economic point of view.
First of all, the cost of machinery is too high. Secondly, too many taxes plague the farmers. They have to pay too many taxes and they pay too much for their machinery. In such circumstances, they cannot do well.
Whatever things the Minister of Agriculture may do or whatever plans he may devise, they prove useless and are no solution to the problems of the farming industry.
We all know that when farmers are well off, the country is prosperous because the farm people are the greatest consumers.
Farmers are the greatest consumers in the world. They have all kinds of needs in various fields and they are responsible for keeping Candian industry going. They ensure the prosperity of the cities and give work to many people in Canada.
So, if we do not encourage agriculture, if we allow it to go slowly to the devil, the rest of the people will also go there.
Never in our history have we experienced such an indifferent, such an unwholesome policy as this one. The minister will say that the government is spending millions for this

Mr. Speaker, I can assure my hon. friend that I am not that well entrenched in my department yet, but I am working on it.
For my money, that was a pretty good beginning for the minister. On Friday, June 13, I questioned the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) again as to what progress he was making, and he admitted that there had been some brief consultations and he hoped to have something to report in a matter of days. Whereupon I suggested this might be a good subject for him and me to discuss some night on the late show. So, here we are.
I am sure the minister will not mind if I say in public that we had one of those conversations in the hall a day or so ago in which he asked me whether I had any idea how many times I had asked questions about pension matters, whether about old age pensions, or veterans pensions, or pensions of retired civil servants, and I admitted to him that it could be hundreds, or perhaps even thousands of times; I had no such record. But 1 want to say to him tonight this is not what matters. What matters now is finding a man of action to get started on this issue.
I do not need to make the case again. The case has been made so often for the right of retired people to keep up with the cost of living and their right to share in increased productivity. The needs of these people are admitted by all. The problem is becoming more acute as time goes on, as people live longer, as inflation gallops a bit faster, and recognition of the fact that something must be done to increase the pensions of those who are already retired is now widespread. It applies, as I have tried to make clear, to pensions of all kinds. It certainly applies to old age pensions in general. It applies to people on private pensions and it applies to peo-[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
pie who have retired on federal pensions-to retired civil servants, retired members of the Armed Forces, retired members of the R.C.M.P. and so on to the group we are talking about tonight, retired employees of Crown corporations and of the C.N.R. in particular. I say a case has been made. The need is there. What is required now, is action. The need is to get started.
I like the appearance, the image the minister has created. Since coming to the Department of Transport he has given the impression of a man who wants to do things, who wants to solve some of the problems, to get moving.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Some day, soon, somebody will have to start the ball rolling in this matter of getting pension increases. Some institutions have done so recently-private corporations and others. I do not know which department will start first in the government-whether it will be to the benefit of the retired civil servants, the C.N.R. pensioners or others. But to show the minister I like him I am giving him the chance to make the start with the C.N.R. retired employees. Yes, the others will have to follow soon-the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), the Solicitor-General (Mr. Mcllraith), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro). But I say to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson): you have the chance to start this, and make a name among retired employees of the C.N.R. and retired people generally.
