subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
subsubtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-LENNOX COUNTY, ONT.-PROTECTION OF RIGHTS OF FARMERS IN EXPROPRIATION PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I bring a matter before the house tonight as a result of a question which I asked last week of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) pertaining to the expropriation of certain lands in the second concession of Richmond township in the county of Lennox and Addington, on both sides of the C.N.R. railway main line, consisting of pieces of contiguous farms owned by six resident owners along a length
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of track of more than a mile. Here, the C.N.R. is expropriating enough land on either side of their present double track right of way to construct a passing siding on their side, the one on the south side to serve the eastbound services and the one on the north side to serve the westbound services of the new proposed automatic central traffic control system which will go into effect in the near future on this important and busy railway.
The first and main point that I wish to make this evening is that the railway, with its lopsided privileges of expropriation, is not being fair to these farmers. First of all, they are offering agricultural prices for the land they require-that is, only $500 an acre-but at the same time they are using the land for industrial purposes, and industrial purposes of national importance as well. Industrial land in and around Napanee, which is in my county, is selling for as high as $1,500 to $2,000 an acre.
At first this railway was a single track line. Then, in the early 1900's it was a double track. Now, in the area where these six farms are located there will be four tracks. Up until now the former 19th century conditions have been tolerated. With the advent of this new system, with its high speed trains, unless proper facilities are provided by the railway these farms, as paying propositions and economic units, are doomed. At the present time there are 16 passenger trains per day operating on this line, plus the four new turbo trains which will soon go into service, together with freight trains both day and night. The railway has not acceded to any request of the farmers for cattle and produce passes underneath the tracks for the safe handling of dairy herds, other livestock pasturing on the opposite side of the railway, and for the safe handling of crops of grain and hay.
Not only is the railroad reducing the value of these farms but it is seriously inconveniencing their future operations. In refusing to construct underpasses for cattle and transportation of agricultural products the railway will endanger the lives of the operators and their livestock and threaten the safety of their equipment. Surface use of this right of way under the proposed conditions will be a very hazardous proposition. Only two weeks ago a farmer whose farm lies along the same railway line 35 miles east in the Joyceville-Gananoque area lost 13 head of very valuable dairy cattle when they were killed by a train as he was frantically trying to drive them across the right of way over
10452	COMMONS DEBATES	June 19, 1969
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion two tracks; and here in Richmond township I am referring to four tracks.
This is now one of the busiest railways on the North American continent. It is reported to me by more than one of the land owners that often less than a minute elapses between the first sight of a train and its passing at the point of observation. This is particularly true when referring to eastbound trains. Although the right of way is fairly straight it has a grade with a horizon that limits westerly visibility in direct proportion to gradient and horizontal distance.
There are several other grievances in connection with this case that 1 can only briefly list and to which the farmers must have an answer. They include: (1) loss of two good wells for watering livestock; (2) the diverting of a natural water course by the C.N.R., namely, Brandon's creek where it crosses the property of Mr. Lipsey, which will be to his disadvantage and will reduce his remaining arable land; (3) the obstruction of crossings by trains in the sidings for extended periods each day.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
As the minister knows I have been in touch with him by letter. Also, I have communicated by telephone with the manager of real estate for the C.N.R. in Montreal. Representations have also been made on behalf of the farmers by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. I ask the minister, as I did in my question of June 11, will he see to it that the economic and human rights of these farmers in Lennox country, whose land is about to be expropriated for railway industrial purposes, are protected and defended.
This matter of expropriation with no assurances or commitments on the part of the railway is most vexing, exasperating and discouraging for these farmers. I recall that many years ago it was trouble between a railway and the farmers of the state of Kansas-the railway disregarded the rights of the ordinary man-that caused Jesse James to turn to a life of revenge and crime that sent him to his doom as an outlaw.
Although the farmers of Richmond township whom I represent are vexed and frustrated, they are not going to pursue the course which Jesse James chose. The farmers of Richmond township are good Canadian
citizens interested in the progress of all Canada, just as much as they are interested in their own progress. All they want in this instance is a fair deal. I appeal to the minister, to the Department of Transport and to the real estate department of the C.N.R. to reopen this case, to give consideration to these land owners and to reassess values pertaining to the land itself as well as drainage problems; the safety problem; the question of cattle and produce passes; the loss of water supply and the diminished value of farms resulting from the widening of the railway. I respectfully request that, for this to be accomplished, an experienced and qualified agronomist who is acceptable to the farmers and the railway be appointed to mediate and adjudicate this case in a manner that will be fair to all parties concerned. The decision of this arbitrator, of course, will be final. I communicated with the real estate department of the C.N.R. in Montreal by telephone this afternoon and I believe they are agreeable to having this problem mediated. Mr. Speaker, in the interests of the just society, here, hopefully, I rest the case with you.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the hon. member's most eloquent representations, not only on this occasion but on previous occasions when he has drawn this matter to my attention, representations on his behalf and on behalf of all these farmers have been made to the C.N.R. It is, of course, a decision for the C.N.R. to make but I have been very happy to urge them to follow the course which the hon. member has suggested. As he was advised this afternoon, I believe, the C.N.R. has now agreed to the appointment of an independent agronomist who will examine the whole picture. His services will be engaged to carry out an in depth study of the entire farm operations of the farmers affected and the total amount of damages which farmers have suffered due to their having to cross the wider railway right of way. He will also express his opinion as to the sum of money required to be paid to each farmer. I hope as a result of this action the matter can be resolved in the interests of the farmers who, I quite agree, have a genuine problem.
